Using China's Plan on Clean Energy Accommodation as a quasi-natural experiment and micro-panel data from the China Family Panel Studies for 2012–2022, we find that the policy reduced residents' out-of-pocket medical expenditure in policy-targeted regions by about 18% on average, with larger reductions among rural residents and in regions facing larger pre-policy accommodation gaps. Consistent with this reduction, supporting evidence indicates that the policy reduced renewable curtailment, increased realized clean electricity output, and improved ambient air quality; it was also associated with cleaner household energy use and more frequent exercise, especially in rural areas. These gains, however, were unevenly distributed, with larger effects in net electricity-exporting and resource-rich regions, areas with limited healthcare service capacity, and among lower-income, male, and middle-aged residents. An illustrative calculation suggests potential annual savings of RMB 261.2 billion (US$38.3 billion) in out-of-pocket medical expenditure across the policy-targeted regions. These findings underscore the importance of clean energy accommodation and provide evidence to inform policies aimed at translating renewable electricity into more equitable household welfare gains.
keywords: China; Clean energy accommodation; Defensive expenditure; Distributional effects; Out-of-pocket medical expenditure; Renewable curtailment

abstract: This study examines the relationship between rural out-migration and local deforestation in Mon State, Myanmar, using a novel panel dataset that combines household-level migration surveys with high-resolution remote sensing observations from 2000 to 2015. Employing dynamic panel estimation methods with a 1000-meter buffer to capture local forest changes, we find robust evidence that out-migration significantly mitigates deforestation at this hyper-local scale, with each additional migrant associated with more than 5 square meters of forest loss reduction per year. Extensive robustness checks, including falsification tests and reverse causality assessments, further reinforce the credibility of our findings. Exploring potential mechanisms, we provide suggestive evidence that remittance income facilitates household energy transitions away from biomass fuels toward electricity, thereby potentially reducing reliance on firewood and charcoal and alleviating local deforestation pressures. By identifying a novel energy-transition channel through which migration may promote environmental sustainability, this study contributes new empirical evidence to the migration–environment literature and shows that out-migration’s environmental effects extend beyond household-size changes to reshape household energy use and land-sustainability pathways in rural frontier regions.
keywords: Deforestation; Energy transition; Myanmar; Out-migration; Remittances; Rural development

abstract: The bioeconomy is a key pillar of the European Green Deal, yet its implementation remains constrained by entrenched linear value chains, fragmented logistics systems, and regulatory uncertainty. This paper examines how practitioners across Europe envision circular bioeconomy transitions, drawing on 43 harmonised multi-actor workshops conducted in 14 countries with 1078 participants from primary production, processing industries, technology provision, public authorities, and civil society. Using a structured participatory canvas and comparative thematic analysis, we analyse how stakeholders redesign existing value chains, which innovation pathways they prioritise, and which barriers they encounter in practice. Across agriculture, forestry, aquatic systems and bio-based industries, stakeholders consistently shift the focus from expanding biomass production toward better use of residues and side-streams. Dominant innovation pathways include residue valorisation, nutrient and water recycling, integrated bioenergy systems, and emerging biomaterials. Four interlinked barrier domains recur across countries and sectors: economic barriers, technological limitations, feedstock logistics and infrastructure constraints, and policy and regulatory challenges. The findings suggest that circular bioeconomy transitions are constrained less by a lack of innovation opportunities than by recurring economic, technological, infrastructural, regulatory, and knowledge-related barriers across countries and sectors. Providing one of the most extensive cross-country, practitioner-led analyses of circular bioeconomy transitions to date, the study offers insight into the conditions shaping circular bioeconomy development across Europe. The findings point to a policy agenda focused on regulatory clarification, coordinated investment in residue aggregation and pre-treatment infrastructure, while highlighting the need for complementary sustainability assessments to evaluate ecological effectiveness and broader socio-ecological implications.
keywords: Bio-based value chains; Bioeconomy policy; Circular bioeconomy; Innovation pathways; Interconnected barriers; Residue valorisation; Stakeholder participation

abstract: Global economic growth has improved living standards but has also intensified environmental pressures on land, air, and water resources. As demand for these resources continues to rise, a central question in sustainability research is whether economic growth can be decoupled from environmental degradation. While a growing body of literature has documented cases of decoupling, most studies focus on individual pollutants, resources, or countries, providing limited insight into whether progress in one environmental domain translates into broader environmental sustainability. This paper addresses this gap by applying a decomposition analysis to greenhouse gas emissions, fine particulate air pollution (PM2.5), land use, and water use across 141 countries over the 2004–2017 period. Using a harmonized global database, the analysis attributes changes in environmental pressures to scale, composition, and efficiency effects and provides a comparative assessment of their relative importance across environmental domains. The results show that improvements in production efficiency have been the primary driver of decoupling, offsetting more than half of the environmental pressures associated with economic growth. However, cases of absolute decoupling remain uncommon and are concentrated largely in high-income countries. Moreover, while many countries achieve decoupling in individual environmental dimensions, simultaneous decoupling across greenhouse gases, air pollution, land use, and water use is exceptionally rare. These findings suggest that technological progress alone is unlikely to deliver broad-based environmental sustainability and highlight the challenges of reconciling continued economic growth with reductions in multiple environmental pressures.
keywords: Composition; Decoupling; Efficiency; Environment and growth; Global analysis; Scale

abstract: We analyse the potential of wealth taxes to reduce CO2 emissions through two transmission channels: the inequality channel, which links reductions in wealth inequality to lower emissions, and the consumption channel, which operates through the effect of wealth taxes on consumption by top wealth holders. We simulate the effects of various wealth tax designs over one- and ten-year horizons using harmonized microdata from 22 European countries. Our analysis accounts for survey non-response bias, heterogeneous rates of returns across households, and behavioural responses to taxation. We find that, through the inequality channel, a recurrent annual progressive wealth tax could reduce annual CO2 emissions by 7.5%–14.7% after 10 years relative to a no-tax scenario, depending on tax progressivity. Through the consumption channel, the average reduction is 1.5%–3.6% after 10 years. In addition, we show that the revenues generated cover the entire investment gap identified by the European Commission's ‘Fit for 55’ emissions reduction programme. These findings highlight the potential of wealth taxes to serve a dual purpose: curbing wealth concentration and contributing meaningfully to climate mitigation and justice, by focusing on high-net-worth households that account for a disproportionate share of emissions.
keywords: Climate policy; CO2 emissions; Household finance and consumption survey; Wealth inequality; Wealth tax

abstract: Human expansion into wildlands has intensified human-wildlife conflicts (HWC), resulting in a need for mitigation. Compensation, a mitigation tool, faces challenges due to underestimated costs, including transaction costs. We developed a framework to identify transaction costs based on successful post-conflict compensation scheme elements, focusing on Verification, Process, and Compensation. As part of this framework, we identified key parameters determining transaction costs. We applied this framework to quantify transaction costs in a human-tiger conflict (HTC) compensation scheme near Pilibhit Tiger Reserve, India, by surveying HTC-affected persons or their families in 2022. Most participants were unaware of the compensation process, found it difficult, and expressed dissatisfaction with government agencies. The average waiting cost at the 2022 USD rate was $583 per claimant, with a 101-day delay, and total transaction costs exceeded 40% of the compensation amount received. Because compensation increased with claimant effort rather than need, awareness, or socioeconomic status, the results point to an equity concern: administrative burdens disproportionately reward those able to navigate costly processes. Therefore, reducing procedural barriers is essential to ensure fair and equitable access to compensation schemes. This framework provides a scalable tool to improve conservation compensation programs globally by identifying interventions that reduce transaction costs, thereby alleviating the impacts of HWCs across diverse regions and species.
keywords: Compensation; Conservation planning; Endangered species; Human-wildlife conflict; Tigers; Transaction costs

abstract: This paper contributes to urban studies debates on the commons-as-practice by examining the “secretly public” musicking spaces co-created by people seeking asylum and allies in Bristol, UK—a city where the language of sanctuary coexists with state-sanctioned forms of slow violence and uneven processes of urban regeneration. The analysis draws on 18 months of ethnographic and participatory research with a group of around 60 men and women of diverse origins, many seeking asylum, who convened weekly music sessions. Building on perspectives that show how sound shapes the sensing, sharing, and reconfiguration of urban space, the study attends to the sonic and affective registers, urban geographies, and (in)visible spaces of sociality that emerged from the group. It argues that “public secrecy” constitutes a condition of possibility for commoning in cities shaped by sanctuary initiatives and state enforcement infrastructures. The paper conceptualises a secretly public commons as a collective practice that composes publicness through thresholds of visibility, generating shared affective, social and material resources while exceeding normative frames of (in)visibility and (un)deservingness that dominate public narratives of asylum. In doing so, this paper extends debates on the urban commons, sanctuary, and sonic urbanism by showing how sonic practices reconfigure public presence under intersecting forms of dispossession, and by using ethnographic and participatory approaches to address what tends to go unnoticed in studies on urban commons and sanctuary urbanism.
keywords: forced migration; musicking; sanctuary urbanism; secretly public communing; urban commons

abstract: Climate-related events such as heatwaves and their impacts on health and wellbeing pose an increasing threat to the future livability of cities. However, in Australia, governance for heat risk management remains less developed than for other climate-related hazards, such as bushfires and floods, and is characterised by fragmented institutional arrangements. This paper examines the formation of the Greater Sydney Heat Taskforce and the co-design of Greater Sydney’s inaugural Heat Smart City Plan as a case through which to interrogate broader challenges in urban climate governance. Drawing on a participatory action research approach, the study analyses how multi-stakeholder governance arrangements emerge in contexts with limited legislative mandate, and how coordination, legitimacy, and shared ownership are constructed across diverse actors. The findings show that while the Taskforce generated progress—improving cross-sectoral understanding, clarifying roles, and building collaborative momentum—significant challenges remain. In particular, unresolved issues relating to resourcing, institutional capacity, and the evolving clarification of governance responsibilities continue to constrain implementation. The paper argues that governance for emerging risks such as extreme heat is shaped not only by formal institutional frameworks, but also by processes of co-design, negotiation, and knowledge co-production, which both enable coordination and challenge existing institutional capabilities. These insights have broader relevance for cities developing coordinated responses to complex climate risks.
keywords: climate change adaptation; co-design; governance fragmentation; Greater Sydney; heatwave; multi-level governance; participatory action research; urban climate governance

abstract: Temporal imagination of urban transformation in Asian cities is predominantly occupied with spectacular rapidity and high density. This singular representation neglects its messy but generative polyrhythmic assembling process and how previous patterns and recurring growth shape imaginations of multiple futures, which inhibits appreciation of the emerging slow growth. This paper employs a rhythmanalytical lens—particularly its repetition-with-difference and polyrhythmic elements—with a focus on density/densification, to examine the shifting development paradigms in Rushan, a small coastal Chinese city struggling to reconfigure its polyrhythms in the slow-growth era. Rushan once witnessed annual repetition of urban growth through selective housing densification capitalising on trans-local investors’ desire for lower-density coastal living, driven by the housing capital rhythm and a pro-growth coalition. Shrinking housing demand and national strategies promoting compact development, however, ushered in a (different) slow-growth period. The rhythms of seasonal investor-residents and tourists, and the transient density they entailed, became key sites for accumulation. Yet their seasonal and fragmented urban engagement produced incomplete and slow(er) development. Two contested futures emerged polyrhythmically: one seeking to fix the slowness through resuscitating housing capital, the other embracing it and the associated transient density, alongside new manufacturing industries’ remedial temporalities of consistency and stability. In so doing, we extend rhythmanalysis beyond repetition, patterning, and everydayness to emphasise difference, impermanence, and emergence, unravelling its co-constitutive relationship with the density-making process. We also call for foregrounding a polyrhythmic logic in dissecting post-growth urban development and re/imagining urban futures through heterogeneous spatio-temporal modality and innovative polyrhythmic reassembling in China and across Asian cities.
keywords: density; polyrhythm; rhythmanalysis; slow development; small city; urban development

abstract: This critical commentary requests creative, critical, and inclusive dialogue about the persistence of inequitable housing and health inequalities. It complements numerous publications in housing and urban studies about environmental, ethnic, socio-economic, and residential inequalities in an era of growing neoliberal politics and policies that influence housing and health inequities. The main aim is to propose conceptual and methodological reforms in housing and urban studies. I posit that critical transdisciplinary inquiry enables innovative contributions to bridge the gap between persistent housing and health inequities and ineffective responses to them. Critical transdisciplinary inquiry includes ethical and moral values that acknowledge and confront housing and health inequities worldwide. The common actor/institutional framework used by academic researchers in housing and urban studies that devalues dominant power imbalances of private investors and property owners in housing markets is contested; the authority of local and national governing institutions to support alternative approaches is revalued. Given the ineffectiveness of private enterprises and public authorities in reducing housing and health inequities since the 1980s, community consortia should be supported to mainstream cooperative housing and expand their effective responses. Lessons from 19th-century housing and urban history, and coordinated responses to the COVID-19 pandemic, support this way forward.
keywords: critical transdisciplinary inquiry; housing and health inequalities; inequity

abstract: The expanding scholarship on ‘caring’ or ‘care-full’ cities has usefully reconceptualised cities as spaces of care and, by exposing real-world local initiatives, compellingly argued in favour centring care in urban governance and planning. Arguably, however, the insufficiently nuanced understanding and use of the concept of scale has weakened the analytical grip of this body of work on how and which practices and relations of care emerge, with which impact and for whom. Relatedly, the subtle but persisting tendency to foreground the urban as the primary site of caring has undercut the possibility to problematise and repoliticise care as a multiscalar field of praxis and intervention. This intervention develops a sympathetic critique of research on urban care, calling for more ‘scalar-attuned’ perspectives that explicitly and reflexively engage with the concept of scale. To illustrate the relevance of our argument, we call for the (re)insertion of the national scale into scholarship on urban caring and highlight three intertwined modalities in which the national co-constitutes care in the city. We do so not to demand top-down state intervention to care, but to invite scholars working on urban caring to consider, discuss and contest the full spectrum of scales-as-relations that constitute the practices and politics of (un)caring.
keywords: care; care-full cities; multiscalarity; scale; the national scale

abstract: Linguistic accessibility, the availability of services and information in languages familiar to residents, remains largely absent from environmental gerontology and age-friendly city assessment frameworks, despite its growing significance for older adults in multilingual cities undergoing rapid language policy transitions. This study develops a framework of neighbourhood linguistic accessibility for older people and applies it to 10 planning areas with high older-adult concentrations in Singapore. Using 3922 points of interest and 31,275 online reviews collected from Google Maps, it constructs dual supply-side (D1) and demand-side (D2) linguistic diversity indices, refined through sentiment analysis to better reflect the linguistic experiences of everyday service use, and analysed through spatial clustering to identify distributional patterns across the urban environment. The results reveal a systematic spatial mismatch: linguistic diversity hotspots concentrate in the Central Business District, while mature estates where more than 25% of residents are aged 65 and above display no comparable linguistic accessibility. Within Singapore’s planning structure, which designates town centres as mixed-use daily service hubs for older residents, linguistic accessibility varies markedly, with only a minority showing meaningful multilingual diversity. These mismatches suggest two mechanisms of linguistic gentrification: globalisation-driven concentration of multilingual environments, and community-renewal-driven displacement of historically inclusive spaces. Identifying four spatial configurations and four differentiated policy categories, the study challenges the assumption that signage diversity equates to accessibility and calls for embedding language–competence alignment within age-friendly assessment frameworks, offering a transferable approach to achieving linguistic equity in multilingual urban governance.
keywords: active ageing; age-friendly cities; ageing-in-place; linguistic accessibility; linguistic gentrification

abstract: Homeownership has long been an important component of housing policy initiatives. U.S. national homeownership has remained relatively stagnant at around 65% from the establishment of the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) in 1965 through the 2020s, prompting discussion about the effectiveness of related policies. Given the limited understanding of long-term housing trajectories, this study examines the trends and geographies of the number of owner-occupied housing units (the Number), homeownership (the percentage of owner-occupied units among all occupied units), population, and households from 1970 to 2020. Nationally, both the Number (39.8 million to 80.1 million) and households (63 million to 126.8 million) roughly doubled, while homeownership remained relatively stable (63.0% to 63.1%). This suggests that sizable expansions in housing stock do not translate into higher homeownership, whereas declines are more likely when housing growth lags behind increases in households. The Number, households, and population were closely related, although population grew more slowly, increasing by about 1.6 times compared with 2 times for the former two measures. Disparities in the Number widened across the country and within states despite stable national homeownership rates. Meanwhile, homeownership exhibited reduced spatial clustering and declines particularly in regions experiencing rapid housing and population growth. Overall, the expansion of the U.S. housing supply broadly kept pace with household growth and accommodated declining household sizes nationally, although regional divergences in homeownership outcomes remained. This study identifies where and when housing divergences emerged and highlights the need to better align housing development with regional and demographic dynamics to support homeownership attainment.
keywords: Affordability; County-level analysis; Housing stock; Housing tenure; Inequality; Population

abstract: This study investigates how urbanization affects the shadow economy in a transitional context, emphasizing the roles of formal firm expansion and local governance quality. Using a panel dataset of 63 Vietnamese provinces over 2006–2021, we employ fixed-effects and System GMM estimators to examine direct, mediating, and moderating effects. The results reveal that urbanization significantly reduces the shadow economy, primarily by stimulating formal firm expansion and registered employment opportunities. Higher local governance quality - particularly stronger corruption control, simplified administrative procedures, greater transparency, and enhanced vertical accountability - also directly constrains informality. Moreover, local governance quality strengthens the formalizing effect of urbanization, indicating that provinces with stronger institutions derive greater benefits from urban growth. These findings suggest that the formalizing impact of urbanization depends critically on institutional capacity and governance quality. By developing a moderated mediation framework linking urbanization, governance quality, and formal firm expansion, this study contributes to the literature on structural transformation, informality, and decentralization, while offering policy implications for managing informality through coordinated urban and institutional reforms in developing economies.
keywords: Formal job creation; Local governance quality; Shadow economy; Urbanization

abstract: Agglomeration policy has long been a dominant paradigm in spatial development, premised on the assumption that large, integrated city-regions drive national economic growth through productivity, innovation, and global integration. This paper examines how this paradigm is reworked under conditions of polycrisis, a durable state in which economic, geopolitical, and institutional shocks interact and reinforce one another. We argue that, while a crisis is often addressed through recalibrating policy tools and objectives, polycrisis reshapes the underlying rationalities of spatial planning. Focusing on Russia, the study analyses how national spatial priorities shift from growth and competitiveness toward territorial stabilisation, population retention, and the management of systemic vulnerability. It compares the 2019 and 2024 Spatial Development Strategies, drawing on policy documents, implementation materials, and expert discussions, and applies a process-tracing approach to reconstruct changes across two planning cycles. The findings show that agglomeration policy is not a universally stable development model but a contingent framework dependent on growth, openness, and functional integration. As these conditions erode under polycrisis, agglomeration policy is reworked from a governance technology of growth into a mechanism of territorial anchoring and control, signalling a broader shift from development to stabilisation in spatial planning.
keywords: Polycrisis; Russia; Spatial governance; Territorial resilience; Urban agglomeration

abstract: This paper presents findings on the relationship between gender and three key housing asset indicators in China: homeownership, second homeownership, and housing asset value. The analysis also considers whether having a son modifies the relationship between gender of the household head and the housing asset indicators. The empirical analysis found that male household heads are more likely to have homeownership, female household heads are more likely to own a second home, and female homeowners tend to own more expensive homes than male homeowners. These findings are robust across alternative functional forms and variable definitions. The results highlight the importance of exploring the differential likelihood of homeownership and second homeownership as well as disparities in housing asset values from a gender perspective.
keywords: Education; Gender gap; Homeownership; Housing asset

abstract: Rural migrant women in urban China commonly face insufficient economic resources and limited opportunities for self-development, which may hinder improvements in subjective well-being (SWB) and foster materialistic orientations. Residential conditions may serve as behavioral and consumption-related manifestations of materialistic pursuits and, in turn, affect SWB. Grounded in the Model of Goal-Directed Behavior (MGB) and based on questionnaire survey data collected in Nanjing, China, this study employs linear regression and mediation analyses to examine how materialism affects SWB among rural migrant women and to test the direct and mediating effects of residential conditions. Social comparison is incorporated as a moderating variable, and moderation analysis is used to assess its role within these pathways. The results show that materialism is significantly negatively correlated with SWB. Regarding residential conditions, both housing tenure and household amenities exert direct effects on SWB, while community type and household amenities mediate the relationship between materialism and SWB. Furthermore, social comparison moderates both the direct and indirect effects of materialism on SWB. The findings suggest that rural migrant women's material pursuits reflect motives of psychological compensation and the pursuit of social recognition, and that constrained gender and institutional identities, together with individual capital, may underlie the adverse consequences of materialism, with residential choices embodying these mechanisms.
keywords: Materialism; Residential conditions; Rural migrant women; Social comparison; Subjective well-being

abstract: Some countries are more prone to crises not only due to their location in a highly volatile region or their macroeconomic weaknesses, but also because of their inherent natural attributes (such as climate conditions, seismic activity, and the presence of wetlands, etc.). The housing sector is highly vulnerable due to its immense size, capital requirements, long investment cycles and sensitivity to external shocks, making it even more fragile in these crisis-prone environments. In building resilience against crises, the role of housing developers -especially within a market-driven residential sub-sector supported by hybrid state interventions- is critical. The aim of this study is to explore how housing developers in a crisis-prone region, such as Istanbul, can strategically adapt to and manage crises through practical urban resilience strategies. Using a methodological approach centered on Structural Equation Modelling (SEM), a survey was conducted with 140 housing developers in Istanbul, Turkey. The sample was selected using a stratified design taking into consideration operational longevity, spatial footprint, and development volume. The model uses 10 latent and 36 observed variables, including internal (scope of activity, structure, brand, working model, network) and external factors (political climate, imbalances, global developments, and social balances) that shape housing developers' resilience. The findings show that resilience depends on internal and external factors, with internal capabilities exerting a higher impact. This reveals that resilience is largely related to organizational capacity, decision-making processes, and corporate strategy. This helps explain corporate responses to crises and the private sector's role in urban resilience.
keywords: Crises; Housing Developers; Istanbul; Resilience; Turkey

abstract: This paper examines Chongqing's state-entrepreneurial governance through two flagship urbanisation policies: Dipiao, or land tickets, and Public Rental Housing (PRH). It defines the Equity through Assetization and Debt (EAD) interlock as a Chongqing-specific mechanism that combines Dipiao-based assetization, debt-backed PRH provision, and central-local mediation within the broader logic of state entrepreneurialism. By the end of 2022, Dipiao transactions had reached 369,000 mu and 72.442 billion CNY, with redistribution mechanisms supporting rural migrants. Since 2010, Chongqing's PRH programme had delivered more than 40 million square metres of affordable housing. The public record supports institutional co-articulation through temporal sequencing and a shared fiscal-land regime, without establishing a dedicated revenue chain from Dipiao receipts to PRH construction. Reliance on volatile land markets and debt financing creates fiscal vulnerabilities, while peripheral PRH siting imposes heavy commuting burdens and sustains socio-spatial inequalities. Using directed thematic analysis of policy documents, audited statistics, and peer-reviewed studies, the paper traces how the three EAD components were assembled, examines their economic and social consequences, and identifies the governance tensions created by land-market volatility, debt service, peripheral siting, and uneven service provision. It offers a mechanism-based refinement of state entrepreneurialism and evidence from an inland Chinese municipality facing growth pressure, fiscal constraints, and equity commitments.
keywords: Central-local mediation; Debt-financed urbanisation; Dipiao; EAD interlock; Public rental housing; State entrepreneurialism

abstract: The spatial relationship between morphological and functional centers influences the efficiency of resource allocation and the coordination of spatial structure. However, existing studies predominantly focus on macro-level trend analysis, lacking not only typological examinations based on their spatial relationships but also investigations into the factors influencing these spatial relationships. Using ASEAN as a case study, this paper identifies its morphological and functional centers, conducts a comparative analysis across different economic development stages, and examines their spatial relationships, typologies, and underlying drivers. The results reveal three key findings: (1) Morphological centers in ASEAN cities generally display polycentric and dispersed patterns, while functional centers tend to be monocentric and concentrated. (2) The spatial linkage between morphological and functional centers is heterogeneous and closely tied to economic development stages. Among these factors, Fragmentation, Transportation, and History remain consistently influential across all stages. In contrast, the influence of Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) and industrial parks exhibits a growing trend during the middle and later stages of economic development. (3) While the number, scale, and spatial relationships of morphological and functional centers vary distinctly across different economic development stages, their spatial distribution characteristics exhibit notable commonalities.
keywords: ASEAN; Functional centers; Morphological centers; Spatial relationship; Stages of economic development

abstract: While internationally condemned, residents of informal settlements around the world continue to face the threat of eviction and displacement. In Asian cities, neoliberal urban development policy has been identified as a key driver of development-inducted displacement. Through the mapping of informal settlement displacement in three megacities in Asia, this paper investigates the spatial and temporal patterns of such displacement in a comparative way. Complemented by policy analysis, the displacement of informal settlements is analysed through trends in the annual distribution of displacement, the spatial concentration around central business areas and waterfronts, their post-demolition land-use, and the scale of individual demolitions. While practices of slum clearance and urban renewal in the three case study cities are all informed by neoliberal urban planning policy, this paper finds that the governance and finance arrangements characterizing each city have a clear impact on the spatiality of informal settlement displacement.
keywords: Asia; Displacement; Eviction; Informal settlement; Mapping; Neoliberal urban development

abstract: We develop an analytical framework of knowledge complementary potential of cities for firms and its innovation effects, and conduct empirical analysis based on 998 listed firms in China. We find that the complementary knowledge (CK) significantly increases the likelihood of technological diversification, and this effect does not exist in isolation but forms a complementary relationship with the firm's knowledge relatedness density. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that the innovation effects of CK vary substantially across different types of firms. In high-tech industries and private firms, the effect relies more heavily on the support of firms' internal knowledge structures; whereas in non-high-tech industries and state-owned firms, CK also exerts a direct promoting effect.
keywords: Cities; Complementary knowledge; Knowledge relatedness density; Multilocational firms; Technological diversification

abstract: In this paper, we combine a nationally representative survey of Canadians with a survey of more than 700 mayors and councillors in municipalities across Canada to explore (a) the extent to which politicians align with their constituents in their housing policy attitudes and (b) the extent to which politicians' views are more representative of more privileged local residents, such as homeowners. We find strong evidence of macrolevel attitudinal congruence: when local communities are more supportive of a housing policy proposals, local politicians tend to be more supportive as well. We also find that politicians' attitudes on housing are not more aligned with privileged local residents; instead, elite-mass alignment is primarily shaped by ideological congruence.
keywords: Housing; Municipal politics; Public opinion; Substantive representation

abstract: Environmental regulation is key to sustainable development, yet its impact on societal wellbeing remains underexplored. This study uses prefecture-level panel data from China (2000−2022) to examine how environmental regulations, both formal and informal, affect wellbeing across cities with varying economic development. Our findings show: (1) formal regulation does not typically enhance wellbeing, while informal regulation positively affects all cities. (2) The impact of formal regulation depends on a city's per capita GDP, supporting the “Porter Hypothesis” in wealthier cities, where formal regulations improve wellbeing, while the opposite occurs in poorer cities. (3) The moderating roles of industrial structure upgrading and employment are identified: they amplify the positive effect of formal regulation in wealthier cities but exacerbate its negative effect in poorer cities. For informal regulation, these two factors consistently serve as positive moderators across all city groups, reinforcing its beneficial effect on wellbeing. This study sheds light on the nuanced role of environmental regulation in promoting sustainable wellbeing in urban contexts.
keywords: China; Environmental regulation; Income group; Wellbeing

abstract: As global shocks become more frequent, strengthening the economic resilience of cities has become a central concern for sustainable urban development and governance. While economic and institutional conditions are widely acknowledged, the role of cultural factors in shaping cities' economic resilience remains underexplored in urban studies and policy debates. This study develops a global city-level gross domestic product (GDP) dataset for 7652 cities across 177 countries by combining monthly nighttime light data with a two-stage machine learning approach. Random forest is first employed in response to the post-2020 shock period, followed by XGBoost to generate high-frequency GDP estimates. Using these data, we evaluate cities' economic resistance, recoverability, and overall resilience to a series of shocks after 2020. Leveraging Hofstede's individualism index and applying OLS regressions with instrumental variable techniques, our results show that individualism has a significant negative effect on all three resilience dimensions. The negative association is more pronounced for recoverability than for resistance. Importantly, strong government regulation and robust infrastructure help to offset this adverse effect. These findings suggest that cultural orientation matters not only for how cities absorb shocks, but also for how effectively they coordinate recovery. By bringing culture into the analysis of global cities' economic resilience, this study extends existing research beyond material and institutional explanations and highlights the importance of governance capacity and infrastructure in culturally diverse contexts.
keywords: Collectivism; Economic resilience; Global; Individualism; National culture

abstract: Amid soaring housing prices and increasing social stratification, issues of housing equity in Chinese cities have become progressively prominent. Previous studies have mostly focused on the formal equity of spatial balance, while neglecting substantial disparities in urban facility accessibility and time costs across social groups. From the perspective of vertical equity, this study introduces the Matthew Effect to examine how the accumulation of socioeconomic advantages intensifies spatial differentiation and the unequal distribution of housing resources, revealing structural inequality among income groups in urban space. Using Nanjing as a case study, this research establishes a time-based evaluation system of urban facility accessibility and applies the multiscale geographically weighted regression (MGWR) model to analyze the spatial heterogeneity of housing prices. Integrating the Theil index with spatial match analysis, it further assesses the vertical equity of facility resource accessibility across different income levels. The results reveal a distinct concentric spatial structure of housing prices: high-income groups cluster in core areas with convenient transportation and abundant educational and environmental resources, while low-income groups are marginalized to peripheral zones with higher commuting costs and limited facilities. Differences in time accessibility to urban facilities further amplify price spillover effects in core areas, aggravating vertical inequity in the housing market. By integrating temporal accessibility analysis with multi-scale spatial modeling, this study advances the theoretical and methodological framework of housing equity and proposes a vertical-equity-oriented housing resource optimization strategy to promote balanced urban facility allocation, prevent resource over-concentration, and foster socially integrated urban development.
keywords: Housing prices; Matthew Effect; Multiscale geographically weighted regression; Spatial differentiation; Time-based accessibility; Vertical equity

abstract: Inter-city cooperation has become a central institutional framework for city-regional development, yet its implications for cultural-symbolic connectivity remain underexplored. Drawing on insights from the policy mobilities literature, this study conceptualizes inter-city cooperation as an institutionalized relational infrastructure that shapes cultural-symbolic mobility within an uneven urban hierarchy. Using data from 41 cities in China's Yangtze River Delta (YRD), we measure cultural-symbolic flows with 250,616 place-name POIs and cooperation intensity with 247,035 government-reported cooperation events identified through natural language processing (NLP). The results show that stronger cooperation is positively associated with greater cultural-symbolic connectivity, operating through strengthened investment linkages, population mobility, and collaborative knowledge innovation. This association is more pronounced among non-adjacent cities, across metropolitan boundaries, and in relationships involving peripheral and non-metropolitan cities. These findings suggest that cultural-symbolic mobility within city-regions is shaped not merely by proximity or market forces but also by formal cooperation arrangements, which foster more inclusive regional integration.
keywords: Cultural-symbolic mobility; Inclusive city-regions; Inter-city cooperation; Natural language processing (NLP)

abstract: While suburbanization remains one of the most extensively studied spatial processes, peri-urbanization has only recently gained comparable scholarly attention. It is conceptualized as a multidimensional and dynamic process capturing rural-to-urban transformations, differing from suburbanization in terms of density, land use, migration patterns, employment structure, and a more dispersed form of urbanization. Peri-urbanization can be understood as an umbrella concept encompassing diverse processes at urban peripheries, including suburbanization, and extending beyond the suburban zone. Although these processes overlap, this article proposes a method for measuring both, enabling the analysis of their spatial relationships using the Warsaw Metropolitan Area (WMA) as a case study and public statistics as a data source. Suburbanization is measured as the inflow of urban residents into the city's outskirts relative to the outflow, while peri-urbanization is assessed using a synthetic indicator – the unweighted mean of normalized variables describing demography, entrepreneurship, employment in agriculture, and infrastructure development. The results show no clear link between peri-urbanization intensity and distance from the city. Three trajectories of urban-to-rural transformation are identified, reflecting different combinations of economic, infrastructural, and demographic transformations. In contrast, suburbanization is more strongly associated with city-centered gravitational forces, with generally increasing intensity with distance from the core, although not in a strictly linear manner. A comparison of both indicators shows that, although they intensify in similar sectors of the WMA, municipalities with the highest and lowest values often do not coincide. The proposed operationalization and analytical framework may be applied to other cities with similar development contexts.
keywords: Peri-urbanization; Rural-to-urban transformation; Suburbanization; Urban sprawl; Warsaw Metropolitan Area

abstract: As AI becomes more embedded in urban systems, the demand for data centers continues to rise. This study analyzes 212 data centers in the U.S., focusing on those operated by major ICT enterprises. We examined key site-selection factors using clustering, suitability scoring, graph-based network analysis, and conditional logistic regression. K-means was selected for clustering. Variables were grouped into environmental and locational site-level factors to generate separate suitability indices. To identify siting determinants, we then estimated conditional logistic regression models, comparing each data center against spatially comparable control locations. The results highlight the complexity of selecting a site for a data center. In general, data centers exhibit spatial agglomeration and gain operational advantages from economies of scale. Clustering analysis grouped sites into six categories, each reflecting distinct locational and environmental patterns. The graph-based network analysis further illustrates the trade-offs companies must make between environmental suitability and operational site-level advantages. Regression results revealed that land use structure, particularly land use diversity and was the most powerful determinant of data center siting. Infrastructural factors, including substation density and proximity to primary roads, as well as the concentration of IT workers, also exhibited strong positive effects. Among environmental factors, lower wind speeds and PM2.5 concentrations positively influenced data center siting, while state-level policy incentives remained statistically insignificant. Our findings highlight the distinctive infrastructural characteristics of these facilities. Acknowledging their widespread operational footprint across diverse urban landscapes, planners must proactively engage with the physical and spatial dimensions of digital infrastructure.
keywords: Data center; Digital infrastructure; ICT enterprises; Site selection

abstract: With urban renewal advancing globally, intensified gentrification and rising living costs are exacerbating displacement risk. However, existing research has rarely examined how renewal-induced cost pressures vary across fine spatial units, where their spatial spillover boundaries emerge, and how housing and consumption costs jointly shape displacement risk. We construct a novel analytical framework integrating Double Machine Learning (DML) for causal inference, sliding-window threshold detection for boundary analysis, and eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI). Our analysis in Shenzhen reveals that urban renewal significantly increases displacement risks by raising the relative market standing of housing rents and catering consumption costs. Specifically, the model estimates that renewal causally elevates the inflation-adjusted relative market standing of housing rents by 5.46% and catering consumption costs by 9.69% within the city-wide distribution. Crucially, the spatial analysis uncovers asymmetric patterns: while rental increases exhibit a clear spillover range of approximately 1103.6 m, no significant spatial boundary was detected for consumption cost changes. Further examination identifies three displacement-risk pathways shaped by renewal's differentiated impacts, highlighting how functional replacement and the relative dominance of the “housing-cost crowding-out effect” versus the “consumption-demand substitution effect” shape displacement risk. These findings not only deepen the understanding of the fundamental processes driving direct and indirect displacement but also bridge a critical gap in conventional theory regarding spatial responsiveness to renewal, providing policymakers with spatially-grounded quantitative evidence to advance the complementary objectives of social equity and inclusive development.
keywords: Displacement risk; Double machine learning; Gentrification; Shenzhen; Urban renewal; XAI

abstract: Temporary land use is commonly understood as an informal, experimental, or bottom-up response to planning rigidity and market uncertainty. This article develops a different perspective by examining how public authorities can actively institutionalize temporariness through the temporal organization of property rights. Drawing on the redevelopment of the Jianyuzhou industrial heritage site in Dongguan, China, it shows how differentiated and time-bounded rights can enable present land activation while preserving public control over future redevelopment. Rather than transferring a coherent bundle of property rights, the arrangement selectively distributes rights to use, operate, generate income, and exit across public authorities, developers, and tenants. This produces a form of state-led flexibility in which operational adaptability is combined with institutional reversibility, allowing the state to retain strategic control over land disposition and redevelopment. At the same time, risks and value-capture opportunities are unevenly distributed, generating what we term asymmetric assetization. The article therefore reframes temporary land use as a mode of urban land governance based on the temporalization and differentiation of property rights. It contributes to debates on temporary urbanism by showing that temporariness can be deliberately designed as a governing arrangement for reconciling short-term activation with long-term redevelopment control.
keywords: Asymmetric assetization; State-led flexibility; Temporary land use; Time-bounded land rights; Urban China

abstract: While global urbanization drives economic development, it imposes significant pressures on urban ecological security and public health, with the expansion imbalance between “gray” built-up areas and “green” ecological spaces being a common challenge. Understanding the coordination of their expansion dynamics is key to sustainable urban health. This study examines four Chinese cities, analyzing the allometric growth relationship between built-up areas and green spaces over three decades, and employs a panel threshold regression model to identify the critical threshold of the green-urban allometric growth coefficient ( b ) that causes a threshold effect on the composite healthy city index. Results show: 1) All four cities exhibit a phased evolution from “scale-priority expansion” to “quality-oriented transformation”. 2) Significant regional heterogeneity exists in allometric growth patterns: Shanghai is “green space expansion-dominated”, Beijing and Haikou are “built-up area expansion-dominated”, and Chongqing is undergoing a “transition-improvement” type toward a more coordinated mode. 3) The panel threshold model reveals a nonlinear marginal diminishing return relationship between b and the healthy city index, with a critical threshold γ = 1.130. Beyond this threshold, the promoting effect remains significant but weakened. 4) The key to regulating the health threshold lies in coordinating ecological endowment, policy interventions, and development stage suitability, with planning foresight and regulatory flexibility being central. This study provides a new analytical framework and quantitative evidence for understanding urban green-built-up expansion dynamics across different development stages, and offers a quantitative benchmark for healthy city policymakers facing similar ecological-development trade-offs to optimize spatial planning and cross the health threshold.
keywords: Allometric growth; Green space; Healthy cities; Panel threshold model; Threshold effect; Urban expansion

abstract: Aspirational demands to improve equity have gained some traction alongside the growth imperative on post-industrial urban policy agendas, but the pressing question of how to expand economic opportunity to people and places ‘left out’ of technology-driven growth remains a pressing puzzle. Adding granularity about the actors involved, the power dynamics that ensue, and the consequences for urban policymaking, comparative institutional research over the past decade suggests that equitable post-industrial development will fail without attention to local politics. The institutional capacity required to implement these types of agendas requires cross sector coalitions that are difficult to build and even more difficult to sustain. Illustrative cases of unsuccessful inclusive innovation in two mid-sized restructuring cities, one in the United States and one in France, indicate that these initiatives failed due to weak engagement from local politicians and the business community, suggesting the need for meaningful participatory incentives. Regardless of differences in national policy context, size and specialization matter: these types of cities must work especially hard for economic reinvention while juggling equity imperatives that vie for attention on local policy agendas.
keywords: Collaborative planning; Equitable economic development; Inclusive innovation; Post-industrial economic development; Urban policymaking

abstract: Sustained mobilization can transform how a city talks about housing without changing how it governs. We ask why progressive discourse and electoral majorities so often fail to reshape administrative practice, using Long Beach, California, where an equity-voicing electorate and council adopted inclusionary language even as code enforcement against immigrant neighborhoods rose twelvefold. Drawing on Bourdieu's bureaucratic field, we theorize the local state as a relatively autonomous field stratified into right-hand (public safety), left-hand (provision), and hybrid (development) positions. That stratification, fixed in place by a council-manager charter and an owner-weighted electorate, generates three mechanisms by which transformations stall at implementation: capture of the discretionary budget, performative layering of inclusionary text atop an exclusionary enforcement core, and buffered autonomy among provision agencies. The framework explains the discourse-implementation gap institutionally.
keywords: Bureaucratic field; Code enforcement; Discourse analysis; Immigrant marginality; Inclusionary housing; Long Beach

abstract: Post-socialist urbanisation in Central and Eastern Europe is often described through common processes of decentralisation, land-market formation and suburban expansion, yet the spatial outcomes of transition have diverged substantially across countries. This study examines how contrasting land-ownership reforms and planning instruments shaped long-term built-up dynamics in six second-tier Polish and Romanian urban regions. Using fine-grained Global Human Settlement Layer data from 1975 to 2020, the study applies time-series clustering to identify recurrent trajectories of built-up expansion and compares their spatial distribution, built-up intensity and population-adjusted land consumption. The results show that both countries experienced dispersed peri-urban growth, but in different forms. Romanian urban regions display faster, more fragmented and more land-intensive post-2000 expansion, especially in the newest and lowest-density classes. Polish urban regions also show dispersed development and weak coordination, but their observed spatial signatures are relatively less atomised and more frequently associated with existing settlement structures. These differences are interpreted as the cumulative outcome of ownership reform, parcel structure and development-right allocation within a broader post-2000 context of housing demand, credit expansion, mobility and infrastructure constraints. The paper contributes to comparative post-socialist urban studies by showing that shared socialist legacies did not produce a single urban-regional trajectory and by linking institutional divergence to micro-spatial, multi-decadal evidence beyond capital-city cases.
keywords: Land restitution; Peri-urbanisation; Post-socialist urban regions; Time-series clustering; Urban sprawl

abstract: This study examines the production and typology of social infrastructure among subdivided-unit (SDU) tenants in Hong Kong, a population marked by housing precarity and spatial poverty. Drawing on participatory mapping and ethnographic diary methods, 101 residents living in Sham Shui Po (a district of Hong Kong) logged 5092 outings over a three-week period, tagging places visited and evaluating them across four dimensions: publicness, biophysical environment, affordance for socialities, and social surplus. Spatial cluster analysis (DBSCAN) revealed five high-frequency clusters concentrated near tenants' homes, while hierarchical cluster analysis (HCA) identified five distinct place typologies. Findings show that informal gathering spaces and commercial spaces in Sham Shui Po—such as fruits shops, traditional herbal tea shops, and other street-level eateries—often outperform formally designated community facilities in generating social surplus and fostering social connection, care, and emotional support for SDU tenants. The study highlights the agency of marginalized residents in co-producing social infrastructure through everyday spatial practices and underscores the limitations of planning paradigms that rely solely on “stated” infrastructure. By foregrounding gendered routines and embedded spatial rhythms, this research contributes to a more context-sensitive understanding of social infrastructure and offers insights for inclusive urban design in high-density cities.
keywords: Hierarchical cluster analysis; High-rise high-density cities; Marginalized group; Participatory mapping; Social infrastructure; Spatial cluster analysis

abstract: Urban villages (UVs), widespread informal settlements across Chinese cities, play a vital role in providing affordable housing; however, their livability remains underexamined. This gap hinders progress toward sustainable and equitable urban development. To bridge the gap, we propose a dual-scale livability assessment framework that integrates macro-level geospatial indicators with micro-level human perceptions of streetscapes. At the macro scale, we evaluate UV livability from four key dimensions: safety, health, convenience, and comfort, with indicators derived from multi-source geospatial data. At the micro scale, we incorporate human-centered visual assessments through a vision-language-model-based multi-agent framework, in which multiple agents interpret street-view images, generate rubric-based scores, and arbitrate scoring discrepancies to quantify perceived environmental quality. We choose Shenzhen, a megacity with diverse UV typologies, as the empirical case. Results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in capturing diverse aspects of livability. The findings reveal a pronounced center–periphery gradient and location-specific trade-offs: centrally located UVs generally have higher convenience but lower comfort, whereas peripheral and mountainous UVs show the opposite pattern. Within the sampled UVs, exploratory evidence further suggests broad perceptual deficiencies in alley-dominated interiors, modest improvements in daylighting and openness associated with greater open-space shares, and broader but moderate advantages associated with commercial streets. The proposed framework provides a cross-sectional diagnostic tool for identifying spatial inequalities in UV livability and offers baseline evidence for differentiated urban renewal. It also holds promise for broader urban applications and contributes to the advancement of United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 11.
keywords: Informal settlements; Livability; Street view images; Sustainable Development Goals (SDG); Urban upgrading; Vision-language models (VLM)

abstract: Current analysis of organized crime in the urban space focuses either on its social or spatial embeddedness. As an alternative, this article develops a socio-spatial perspective that recognizes and situates the lived experience of organized crime within urban transformation processes. I developed this perspective by building on ethnographic data about drug trafficking in Barcelona's El Raval, which I examine through the lens of the residents. I focus specifically on the interpretative framework of the “narco-especulació” which links the expansion of the narcopisos phenomenon to rampant speculative practices of real-estate-investors and city-led urban regeneration processes. I argue that this framework articulates a critique of urban governance, underscoring the dispossession of residents' social control, a weakened sense of place, and the fragmentation of community relationships. I also show how this framework can foster collective resistance strategies that express community agency against organized crime while disrupting the ongoing process of urban transformation and public management.
keywords: Community organizing; Ethnography; Housing financialization; Organized crime; Resistance strategies; Urban renewal

abstract: Population decline and rapid aging are placing growing pressure on local governance, yet evidence remains limited on whether targeted fiscal transfers are associated with slower deterioration in shrinking regions. South Korea's 2021 Depopulation Area program provides a nationwide setting to examine this question. Using a district-level panel covering 2012–2024, this study estimates event-study and dose–response models linking local outcomes to designation timing and per-capita fund intensity. Because designation and funding intensity reflect targeted allocation, the estimates are interpreted as diagnostic evidence on relative post-designation trajectories rather than causal treatment effects. Population growth and youth net migration show no statistically detectable association with observed funding intensity over the short post-funding period, consistent with demographic inertia. The most stable pattern concerns housing vacancy: higher funding intensity is associated with lower vacancy rates within districts, a result that persists across exposure-timing, treated-only, baseline-vulnerability, and pre-allocation vacancy-change diagnostics. Associations for housing-stock aging and fiscal self-reliance are more specification-sensitive. Heterogeneity analyses suggest stronger vacancy-related adjustment in structurally vulnerable districts, although these subgroup patterns warrant cautious interpretation. Taken together, the results are consistent with selective functional buffering under structural demographic decline, most clearly in vacancy outcomes, while providing no evidence of short-run population reversal.
keywords: Fiscal transfers; Housing vacancy; Local governance; Place-based policy; South Korea; Urban shrinkage

abstract: Metropolitan functional structure is commonly inferred from population-wide mobility flows, but the extent to which this representation is shared by different socioeconomic groups remains unclear. We address this question using harmonized Origin-Destination household travel surveys for the São Paulo Metropolitan Region in 2007, 2017 and 2023. Weighted directed networks were constructed for five income quintiles and the aggregate population and evaluated using complementary network indicators, permutation tests, bootstrap intervals and equal-person rarefaction. Lower-income networks were consistently sparser, more compartmentalized and characterized by lower duration-based reachability, whereas higher-income networks contained more direct interzonal connections and weaker community separation. The functional-center sets of the poorest and richest quintiles overlapped by less than 10%, and none of their ten highest-PageRank zones coincided in 2023. These differences were persistent but not static: community compartmentalization was the most durable socioeconomic distinction, while connectivity gaps narrowed and centrality concentration changed more substantially. Aggregate networks also represented income groups unevenly, exhibiting consistently lower center-set similarity with the poorest quintile than with upper-income groups. The findings reveal a socially differentiated polycentricity in which multiple centers exist but do not constitute the same functional metropolitan system for all populations. Income-disaggregated networks therefore complement aggregate representations and provide a planning-relevant basis for evaluating metropolitan integration beyond population-wide averages.
keywords: Functional polycentricity; Longitudinal analysis; Socioeconomic inequality; São Paulo; Urban mobility networks

abstract: High-density urban agglomerations face increasing ecological risks from rapid development and carbon pressure. However, ecological resilience is often assessed as a single index, with limited attention to its internal components and carbon-related constraints. We evaluated ecological resilience in 27 cities of the Yangtze River Delta urban agglomeration from 2000 to 2023 by decomposing it into ecological potential, stability, and elasticity. Multi-source spatial and socioeconomic data were analyzed using correlation analysis, random forest–SHAP interpretation, and structural equation modelling. Ecological resilience increased overall but showed substantial spatial heterogeneity. Changes in resilience were strongly and negatively related to baseline conditions in 2000 (R2 = 0.972), indicating a pronounced catch-up pattern in which initially less resilient cities generally achieved greater improvements. Resilience was more closely associated with vegetation-based carbon capacity than with population or total carbon emissions. Forest carbon storage was positively correlated with resilience in both 2000 ( r = 0.70, p < 0.001) and 2023 ( r = 0.64, p < 0.001), whereas population and carbon emissions showed weak overall correlations. Predictor importance nevertheless shifted over time. Per-capita carbon carrying capacity was the leading predictor in 2000, while carbon emissions became the dominant predictor by 2023 and exerted increasingly negative effects at high emission levels. Structural equation modelling showed that forest carbon storage strongly enhanced ecological elasticity in both years ( β = 0.90–0.91, p < 0.001), which remained the principal pathway supporting resilience. These results indicate a transition from vegetation-driven ecological asset building toward carbon-constrained resilience management. Future improvement will require structural decarbonization, ecological corridor protection, and differentiated governance tailored to city-specific resilience conditions.
keywords: Carbon carrying capacity; Ecological resilience decomposition; Forest carbon storage; Structural equation modelling; Urban agglomeration

abstract: Accessible and well-designed public charging points are key elements towards the wider adoption of electric vehicles (EVs), highlighting the need to understand user preferences. This study examines public charging choices of 300 EV users and 288 non-EV users in Great Britain through a stated choice experiment and latent class modelling. Results revealed two distinct segments within each user group. Among EV users, a larger segment prioritised charging price, while a smaller one valued waiting time, charging speed, convenience, available amenities, and high station ratings. By contrast, both non-EV segments remained sensitive to charging price and waiting time, including the larger service-oriented segment. These patterns align with Rogers' Diffusion of Innovation Theory, highlighting behavioural and socio-demographic variations in readiness to engage with public charging infrastructure. The findings provide practical guidance for developing more inclusive and targeted public charging infrastructure that improves user experiences, lowers adoption barriers, and supports the broader shift towards electric mobility.
keywords: Electric vehicles; Great Britain; Latent class model; Public charging choices; Segmentation

abstract: In recent years, there has been growing popularity in urban policies that prioritize pedestrians by reallocating road space away from motorized vehicles, with a focus on active transportation such as walking and cycling, as well as public transit. However, there is limited research exploring the traffic implications of such policies. New York City's (NYC) Open Streets Program, launched in April 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic, aimed to provide outdoor respite and expand access to public space by closing or restricting traffic on select streets. While prior research has suggested health-relevant impacts of Open Streets programs on physical activity, social cohesion, and noise, their impact on local traffic is not well understood. Therefore, we conducted a propensity score–matched difference-in-differences analysis at the census tract level using highly spatially resolved, NYC-wide crowdsourced monthly average daily traffic data. Comparing traffic for census tracts pre-implementation (2019) and post-implementation (2021) of Open Streets, we found an average 13.4% reduction (95% CI: −17.9%, −8.9%) in traffic in tracts with Open Streets compared to pretreatment levels. Moreover, we observed a reduction in traffic (−0.42%, 95% CI: −0.51%, −0.33%) with each percentage point increase in contiguous treated census tracts, suggesting that traffic reductions may be greater where Open Streets are clustered. This study offers insights into the application of a robust research method for evaluating the environmental outcomes of road space reallocation schemes. Additionally, it contributes to understanding the effectiveness of Open Streets in reducing local traffic exposure and informs policy design to create more pedestrian-friendly and healthier urban neighborhoods.
keywords: Built environment; Car-free zones; Open Streets; Policy evaluation; Traffic; Urban mobility; Urban planning

abstract: Urban analytics has developed as an interdisciplinary field to understand and address urban complexity. Despite rapid growth, the field remains fragmented, lacking conceptual clarity and interdisciplinary dialogue. This paper presents a comprehensive systematic review of 427 publications across relevant disciplines. Information about publication details, publication type, research objectives, research fields, methods, main data and data source, data accessibility, data representativeness, geographical and temporal scopes, ethical concerns and policy implications of each study are extracted and categorised. The following analysis traces the evolution of urban analytics, identifies methodological or thematic paucity in current research, and evaluates whether existing studies have approached urban issues in methodologically sound, ethical, and appropriate ways. The findings reveal persistent challenges in definitional contestation, data “firehose” and flood of bias, interdisciplinarity, fragmentation and uneven integration, as well as institutional and practical limits. This review further identifies emerging directions that integrate theory and practice, support responsible innovation, and promote more actionable insights for urban analytics. It also contributes a conceptual framework and research roadmap for developing responsible, context-aware and practical urban analytics that support equitable and sustainable urban futures.
keywords: City analytics; Computational urban science; Urban analytics; Urban big data analytics; Urban data science; Urban informatics; Urban system analysis

abstract: As core recipient regions for industrial transfer in the middle reaches of the Yellow River in China, Shanxi, Shaanxi, and Henan face not only inter-provincial competition but also deeper structural imbalances and coordination dilemmas, highlighting the need to construct a balanced and highly interactive collaborative network. To systematically characterize the regional industrial coordination pattern, this study uses industrial policy text data from 2012 to 2024 to construct a three-layer policy network consisting of policy issuance, policy implementation, and governance-chain layers. Furthermore, competition and complementarity matrices are introduced to examine the evolutionary structure of industrial transfer competition among the three provinces. The findings reveal that while the macro-level policy network exhibits a trend toward cross-provincial coordinated evolution, the micro-level implementation chains remain deeply fragmented. Meanwhile, homogeneous competition exhibits a significant distance-threshold effect, suggesting that geographical distance constrains industrial isomorphism only within certain spatial ranges. Consequently, inter-provincial competition is characterized by parallel competition across multiple industrial channels and structural congestion in key sectors. Additionally, intense external competition in core industrial sectors triggers multi-agency overlapping responses and internal attrition within local implementation systems. In light of these findings, this study proposes mitigating institutional friction by establishing a dedicated intergovernmental consultation mechanism, promoting Smart Specialization in industrial positioning, and implementing a lead-department accountability system.
keywords: Coordination dilemmas; Industrial transfer; Multi-layer policy network; Regional coopetition; Shanxi-Shaanxi-Henan Region

abstract: Public transport underuse is commonly attributed to service quality, accessibility, travel time, cost, and individual preferences. These explanations say less about how travellers evaluate public transport within mobility environments already organised around established modes and practices, and may treat categories derived from particular transport histories as universally applicable. In Ho Chi Minh City, fixed-route buses operate within a motorcycle-based mobility ecology that supports direct access, flexible routing, intermediate stops, trip chaining, and rapid adaptation to changing circumstances. Elastic mobility refers to the adaptive capacity generated by such an ecology, while elastic mobility mismatch describes the difficulty of reproducing that capacity through another transport system. The study draws on 42 brief, open-ended intercept interviews conducted at 11 bus stops, supplemented by field observations. A hybrid deductive–inductive thematic analysis identified four interrelated sources of friction: spatial and access, informational, temporal, and functional. Participants valued buses for their affordability, comfort, and protection from traffic and weather, especially when direct routes matched stable routines. Bus travel became less viable when journeys required uncertain waiting, transfers, intermediate stops, trip chaining, or rapid responses to changing circumstances. The coordination required across a complete journey can reduce the perceived viability of public transport within an established mobility ecology; bus underuse is not simply a failure to adopt a supposedly more advanced mode. Treating HCMC as a source of conceptual knowledge also opens a decolonising conversation about how mobility transitions are understood. The small, non-probabilistic sample supports the identification of this mechanism but not an estimate of its prevalence.
keywords: Decolonising transport knowledge; Elastic mobility; Elastic mobility mismatch; Ho Chi Minh City; Mobility-system compatibility; Motorcycle-based mobility

abstract: Debates on informal settlements often portray slums as spaces of uniform deprivation, obscuring internal variations in socio-economic trajectories, housing investment, and residents' aspirations. Drawing on the conceptual distinction between slums of hope and slums of despair, this study re-examines household survey data collected in Ashaiman, Ghana to assess the settlement's position along a continuum of hope, despair, and transition. Using a multidimensional set of indicators capturing livelihood dynamics, housing consolidation, tenure security and social capital, the analysis provides an integrated assessment of informal settlement trajectories. The findings indicate that while Ashaiman continues to face significant infrastructural and environmental constraints, most households exhibit characteristics consistent with a transitional settlement, combining elements of economic agency and social resilience with persistent vulnerabilities, particularly in relation to tenure security. By moving beyond binary classifications, the study highlights the value of incorporating both objective conditions and lived experiences into slum analysis and contributes to broader debates on urban informality and socially sustainable urban development in the Global South.
keywords: Ghana; Housing tenure security; Slums of despair; Slums of hope; Urban informality

abstract: This study reconstructs the land-use evolution of Tashkent, Uzbekistan, across three benchmark years—1990, 2010, and 2025—using GIS analysis of archival maps, satellite imagery, and open geospatial data. The analysis identifies three broad phases: a compact, functionally zoned Soviet city in 1990; a transitional landscape shaped by emerging market influences in 2010; and a phase of state-coordinated metropolitan expansion by 2025, including the incorporation of territories associated with the New Tashkent City project. Residential, commercial, and transport land uses expanded substantially, while peri-urban agricultural land declined. Rather than a linear post-socialist transition, the findings suggest a sequence of institutional reorderings through which different forms of urban coordination shaped development over time. The case highlights the importance of administrative boundary change and strategic spatial planning in metropolitan growth and underscores the value of incorporating Central Asian experiences into comparative debates on post-socialist urbanism.
keywords: Central Asia; Metropolitan expansion; Post-socialist urbanism; State coordination; Urban land-use change

abstract: Much of the NIMBY literature explains why residents oppose controversial facilities and often treats self-interest as a core driver of local resistance. We shift the focus from opposition to engagement by examining citizens' willingness to co-design in contested siting contexts. Drawing on a vignette experiment in urban South Korea centered on a proposed mental health rehabilitation facility, we test whether motivational framing shapes willingness to co-design, comparing a proximity-based self-interest frame (“in front of my home”) with a broader community-interest frame (“in my city”), and we assess the role of participation self-efficacy.
