Engaging Richard Alba’s scholarship on assimilation and immigrant vitality, it demonstrates how immigrant agency can reconfigure urban futures beyond traditional gateway-city narratives across the contemporary United States and West Texas.
keywords: cultural enrichment; economic revitalization; Immigrant entrepreneurship; social cohesion; urban policy

abstract: This paper examines spatial and gender disparities in rental affordability among young adults (age 18–35) in the city of Buenos Aires. Using a Quantile Regression Forest algorithm, we generate a 20-meter resolution rental price map and combine it with income data disaggregated by sex, age, and quintile to estimate potential access to the rental market under three income-allocation thresholds (30%, 50%, and 70%) and to measure inequity in urban access with the Gini coefficient. Results show that young women face systematically greater restrictions than men: allocating 30% of income to rent, 25.4% of the city is unaffordable to women, versus only 2.6% for men, a gap that widens sharply among those 18–23 years olds (78.3% versus 5.7%). Variable importance analysis indicates that the socioeconomic composition of the neighborhoods, rather than access to urban facilities, is the strongest predictor of rental prices. The study concludes that these gender gaps are structural, rooted in labor-market wage disparities rather than housing prices alone, and proposes a replicable, high-resolution methodology for identifying pockets of spatial exclusion and informing targeted housing policy.
keywords: Affordable housing; gender; inequality

abstract: This article examines the secondhand solar photovoltaic (PV) market of Bhojpur Dharampur, a small town in western Uttar Pradesh, India, where discarded panels are repaired, adapted, and resold to underserved rural households and small businesses. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork conducted between 2019 and 2026, including interviews with wholesalers, resellers, and customers, it shifts the focus from what discarded solar objects become to what their afterlives make. Building on a local history of scrap trading and Muslim biradari kinship ties, traders combine repair, voltage adaptation, storage, warranties, credit, reputation, and resale networks to convert the material ruins of India’s energy transition into workshops, commercial streets, jobs, and a specialized regional market. The article contributes to debates on repair, energy justice, and subaltern urbanization by showing that small-town centrality can emerge not only from demographic growth or industrial relocation, but also from the situated reworking of discarded infrastructures produced elsewhere. Yet the same circuits that provide affordable electricity and livelihoods also concentrate materials that cannot be repaired, resold, or safely recycled. Solar repair thus supports urban specialization while redistributing residual ecological exposure onto already marginalized peripheral towns.
keywords: Asia; geography; urbanization

abstract: This multiple case study explores how and why differences in the availability of affordable rental housing occur at the neighborhood level. Privatizing affordable housing programs for low-income households has complicated and diversified the current U.S. system of affordable housing provision. Multiple players participate in affordable housing provision, including governmental and nongovernmental entities and traditional and nontraditional housing providers. In this context, based on the Neighborhood Governance Framework, this research documents and examines possible reasons for varied outcomes in affordable housing provision, focusing on neighborhoods’ historical contexts, the roles of organizations, and neighborhood governance. I selected four neighborhoods in Columbus, Ohio, with different leading entities: nonprofit, for-profit, public organization, and civil society. Semi-structured interviews with staff from relevant organizations and residents highlight the opportunistic nature of the current affordable housing provision system. They also emphasize the critical roles of a dedicated leading organization, its leadership, and civil society in affordable housing provision. This study illustrates that neighborhood governance with a nonprofit organization dedicated to affordable housing provision (Community Housing Development Organization) demonstrates a persistent model of affordable housing provision, which has a shared objective of stakeholders—maintaining at least 15% of all housing units as affordable housing units.
keywords: Affordable housing; governance; organizations

abstract: Although research on local sustainability initiatives has become increasingly common, relatively little is known about whether sustainability engagement is associated with distinct long-term patterns of change. This study examines socioeconomic and demographic change in 1,340 U.S. cities between 2009 and 2023. Results indicate that cities with the highest levels of sustainability engagement experienced significantly greater increases in median household income, home values, and rents than other municipalities, while differences in poverty reduction, educational attainment, homeownership, and demographic change were modest. Cluster analysis identified four developmental trajectories, with high sustainability-engaged cities disproportionately concentrated within a High-Growth/High-Cost trajectory characterized by strong income growth and rapid housing market appreciation, while being underrepresented within a Lagging Growth trajectory. Among the three pillars of sustainability, environmental sustainability exhibited the strongest association with developmental trajectory. In addition, baseline income inequality was independently associated with subsequent income growth and housing market appreciation after controlling for sustainability engagement and other municipal characteristics. Collectively, these findings suggest that sustainability engagement is associated with distinctive patterns of urban development but likely operates within broader structural and market contexts.
keywords: cities; public policy; Sustainability

abstract: Cities are experiencing new forms of pressure as tourism-related services concentrate in specific areas with limited space and resources, posing challenges for urban planning and land-use regulation. While the concentration of tourism accommodation has been widely examined, less attention has been devoted to understanding how urban form characteristics interact with the spatial distribution of tourism-related services and how these patterns evolve over time. This paper addresses this gap by analyzing Bilbao, a post-industrial city that has transformed into an urban tourism destination. By integrating urban morphology with tourism-service indicators, the study develops a spatiotemporal framework to examine the interaction between Tourism Exposure and Tourism Pressure. In addition, it constructs a cartographic time series to identify the evolution of Tourism Saturation patterns at the city-block scale. The findings suggest that Tourism Saturation does not spread randomly throughout the city but instead emerges through the reinforcement of established tourism hotspots. Furthermore, the temporal analysis reveals a growing spatial selectivity in the distribution of tourism services, leading to higher levels of tourism saturation within the historic core. As urban tourism continues to evolve, the study offers valuable evidence for policymakers seeking to design place-specific strategies to manage tourism in highly exposed areas.
keywords: Bilbao; Spatiotemporal analysis; tourism saturation; tourism services; urban form

abstract: This article draws on Ethiopia’s record of 23 documented capital centers across two millennia to develop a spatial-energetic framework for explaining transitions between mobile and fixed political centers. Capitals accumulate institutional mass that favors persistence, while environmental, geopolitical, and demographic pressures generate countervailing forces; processual conditions determine whether those pressures can be translated into actual movement. The Ethiopian case also challenges a foundational assumption in urban political geography: political centrality does not require permanent built form. Itinerant royal camps concentrated administrative, ceremonial, commercial, and military functions while remaining fully mobile—demonstrating that fixity and centrality are analytically separable properties of political capitals, not necessary complements. A comparative discussion of imperial China, Buganda, Rwanda, and modern planned relocations establishes the framework’s scope and transferability. The revised methodology distinguishes directly coded primary texts from secondary synthetic sources, specifies an outcome-independent ordinal decision rule to reduce post-hoc interpretive bias, and employs four historical territorial reconstructions to assess capital locations against contemporaneous geographic centroids.
keywords: Capital mobility; Ethiopia; institutional inertia; political geography; urban centrality

abstract: Government investments in transit can be a catalyst for gentrification and displacement. Using Maryland’s under construction Purple Line light rail project as a case study, we add evidence to recent debates on the extent of displacement due to transit construction. Our approach is novel in two ways: first, we study the pre-operative phase, as the Purple Line is currently under construction. Second, we utilize a large consumer reference dataset of household addresses, over the period 2006–2022 in the immediate Washington, DC, metropolitan area, to track the impact of the Purple Line’s announcement and construction on displacement. We find some limited evidence of displacement immediately around under-construction Purple Line stations, although the comparison groups in our triple-difference model reveal increased mobility among some low-income renters near established WMATA stations without future Purple Line service. Results are broken down by income quartile, which enables a fine-grained analysis of transit-induced gentrification which illuminates a nuanced reality dependent on local context. These results suggest that anti-displacement measures must be in place well in advance of transit station openings to mitigate against potential displacement.
keywords: Displacement; gentrification; transit

abstract: Low-income coastal waterfront settlements are widely viewed as spaces of risk, informality, and deficit, as the assets that sustain everyday life within these perils remain underexplored in urban resilience research. Yet the role of these social, spatial, and livelihood assets in shaping community resilience has largely remained overlooked and understudied. Using evidence from Rasulpur, a vulnerable waterfront settlement in southwestern Bangladesh, this research aimed to construct an asset-based community resilience framework. It examined both its socioeconomic and spatio-environmental vulnerabilities and available assets. It used a qualitative approach that included observation, interviews, community narratives, and spatial analysis, and analyzed five corresponding asset categories: physical, economic, natural, human, and social. The findings show that vulnerability and asset are not separate conditions but overlapping realities embedded within the same waterfront spaces. While the physical and economic conditions appear the most problematic, natural, human, and social assets provide important bases for adaptation and transformation. Finally, the findings are translated into key resilience principles and a schematic waterfront strategy, offering a spatially grounded, practice-oriented framework for asset-based coastal community resilience.
keywords: asset-based development; Coastal settlements; informal settlements; urban resilience; waterfront

abstract: The term “urbicide” has been used to describe the physical and material destruction of cities, specifically as a means to annihilate the material foundations of heterogeneity. Yet the act of physical destruction often works in tandem with parallel practices of construction that seek to create alternative urban futures. In this paper, we argue that “urbicidal planning” is a recurring logic of planning practice even in cases that do not involve the wholesale destruction of infrastructure. Often, such planning rests on a socio-spatial discourse that targets specific racial, ethnic, or social groups and their corresponding geographies as threats to political and developmental goals. It is therefore a preventative logic of city-making that rests on the eradication of particular urban risks, motivated by the need to pacify or eliminate the present and future dangers of the city. Moreover, it is a preemptive form of eradication that is often dissociated across time and space. We demonstrate these arguments through two illustrative vignettes: the policies and practices of the French protectorate in Morocco in the early 20th century and those of foreign humanitarian and military actors in Haiti during the United Nations’ peacekeeping operation in the beginning of the 21st century.
keywords: cities; Urban planning; urban politics

abstract: Urban areas are becoming strategic sites in the ongoing sustainable energy transition, driven by the new opportunities and imperatives presented by decentralized sustainable energy technologies. However, the presence of cities in the global clean energy landscape remains underwhelming. Despite national programs encouraging urban energy transition in India, the response has largely failed to meet the goals. The existing literature has primarily attributed this to a lack of technical and financial capacity and to the limited legislative role of urban governments. This paper deepens these arguments and offers a more layered view through the case study of Surat in Gujarat, India. I argue that India’s clean energy transition is unfolding within the traditional frameworks and templates that propped up the conventional energy systems, entrenching incumbent power hierar chies. Increasing institutionalization is leading to increased centralization, narrowing the scope of participation for newer actors, including local urban governments. Surat’s case study demonstrates that city governments are keen to respond to local challenges by capitalizing on the opportunities presented by sustainable energy sources. However, the enduring success of their initiatives will depend on supportive agential, structural, and institutional reforms initiated by the powerful elites within India’s energy governance landscape.
keywords: governance; Urban politics; energy transition

abstract: Current neighborhood planning and policy often rely on the delineation of neighborhood boundaries. However, this reliance can marginalize various groups, particularly racial identities, whose definitions, experiences, and perceptions of where they live may diverge significantly. In a changing area of Detroit, we conducted 46 semi-structured interviews in which residents named, drew, and described their neighborhood. Our findings revealed a stark contrast: While most white residents drew boundaries defined by historic designations, developers, or the city government and often used broad, generalized descriptions, many Black residents did not identify with the concept of neighborhood altogether. Instead, they defined community through organizations such as block clubs and described the area with detailed personal narratives. This study demonstrates how administrative maps of neighborhoods often reify the spatial privilege of wealthy, white-defined areas while rendering invisible Black-defined areas that have nevertheless cultivated their own localized governance, community, and identity.
keywords: community; Neighborhoods; race

abstract: The environment in which people spend their lives influences their health behaviours and health outcomes. Traditional studies often use fixed descriptions and ad hoc analyses to characterise environmental exposures at static locations, relating a single environmental factor to one health aspect, even though both the environment and the exposures of people who move through it are dynamic. We introduce a digital twinning approach that semantically integrates ontological concepts and data across environmental features into machine-readable knowledge, enabling scalable and context-aware assessment of individual exposures. This work is built on The World Avatar project, which aims to create an all-encompassing digital twin based on a dynamic knowledge graph. The proposed approach deploys a computational agent to calculate exposures based on semantic representations of environmental features in time and space. The time-specific part of the exposure calculation considers both the historical context (i.e. whether features of the environment had been built) and current context (i.e., whether something was open or accessible) of the exposure. The scalability of the approach is illustrated through the construction of interoperable digital twins and the analysis of smartphone data describing movements in both the UK and Singapore. The resulting exposures capture historic year-specific changes in greenspace and time-specific accessibility based on opening hours of the food retail environment. This approach could facilitate large-scale digital studies, yielding critical insights that help create healthy cities.
keywords: Dynamic environmental exposure; Scalability; Semantic interoperability; Temporal and spatial context-aware

abstract: People experience cities through their senses of sight, hearing, smell, touch, and taste. However, most research focuses only on visual stimuli. In this study, we develop a straightforward multi-sensory, data-based linear regression model to explain human sentiment in cities through visual, acoustic, olfactory, and tactile explanatory features. We use social media to reflect people's sentiments, and concurrent urban environmental data ranging from street view imagery to air quality, collected in the Bronx, New York. We observe correlations between non-visual features and urban experience, where noise and thermal comfort are identified as significant impact factors. The adjusted coefficients of determination for the simple linear models can reach 0.80 and 0.60 for positive and negative sentiments, respectively, indicating moderate to strong interactions between multi-sensory urban features and human sentiments.
keywords: Mobile sensing; Multi-sensory sentiments; Social media; Urban physical environments

abstract: Cities are most often categorized by population size, a continuous indicator that captures scale but does not distinguish internal structural organization. Yet structural typologies require discrete representations of how urban components are arranged and connected. Here, we construct directed networks of dominant interactions among intra-urban centers for more than 9400 cities worldwide, transforming internal organization into comparable topological configurations. We show that urban center-to-center networks occupy a highly restricted subset of theoretically possible configurations. As the number of centers increases, cities do not reorganize arbitrarily but expand through nested, incremental extensions of smaller network configurations. This structural regularity gives rise to a small repertoire of recurrent configurations, enabling a discrete classification of cities based on their internal organization. Beyond typology, we show that structural properties of center networks, including size, breadth, and depth, scale sublinearly with urban population, establishing a quantitative link between internal organization and city size. By shifting the focus from aggregate size to structural configuration, this framework offers a globally consistent and interpretable basis for comparing cities across regions.
keywords: Center networks; Scaling laws; Urban structure

abstract: Spatially explicit machine learning (SEML) models have recently been developed to address spatial heterogeneity and non-linearity. However, many existing SEMLs require post-hoc interpretability methods to extract the functional relationships between independent and dependent variables. Essentially, this type of SEMLs remain approximations derived from prediction outputs rather than from direct estimation of variable contributions, propagating prediction errors and potentially leading to biased interpretations of spatially varying processes. Additionally, SEMLs often face a trade-off between capturing non-linearity and spatial heterogeneity, meaning that a greater focus on non-linearity may reduce the capability of capturing spatial heterogeneity, and vice versa. These limitations constrain their ability to interpret geographical phenomenon. This study proposes a hybrid multiscale geographically weighted XGBoost (HMGWX), which integrates geographically weighted XGBoost (GWXGB) and geographically XGBoost (GXGB) within a semi-parametric additive model framework. The model assigns the most appropriate local estimator (GWXGB or GXGB) for each response-predictor relationship, balancing the ability to address non-linearity and spatial heterogeneity. HMGWX directly estimates the marginal contribution of each variable, thereby avoiding post-hoc errors propagated from prediction outputs. We validate HMGWX using both a synthetic dataset with known parameter surfaces and non-linear relationships, and a real-world ride-hailing waiting time dataset. Results show that HMGWX outperforms traditional spatially varying coefficient models (e.g., multiscale geographically weighted regression, Geographical Gaussian Process Generalized Additive Model) and existing SEMLs (e.g., XGBoost, Geographical-XGBoost, GWXGB, and GXGB) in both interpretability and predictive accuracy when spatial heterogeneity and non-linearity coexist. Compared with the baseline models, HMGWX reduces root mean square error by at least 8%. Furthermore, by introducing spatial clustering, early stopping, and dynamic bandwidth shrinking, we improve the computational efficiency of the calibration procedures for GWXGB, GXGB, and HMGWX, reducing total training time by over 76%. Finally, we propose an evaluation route map to guide appropriate model selection in practice.
keywords: Geospatial artificial intelligence (GeoAI); Interpretability; Non-linearity; Spatial heterogeneity; Spatially explicit machine learning

abstract: Spatial analysis depends upon accessible, flexible tools. As a leading language for data science, Python requires reliable packages to handle complex geospatial tasks effectively. This article presents GeoPandas, a package providing a high-level, user-friendly API that extends standard pandas data structures to support vector geometries, simplifying spatial data handling for a broad scientific audience. The package is built around three core data structures (GeometryArray, GeoSeries, and GeoDataFrame) that unify geometric operations and tabular data management. It achieves performance and scalability by wrapping fast, compiled libraries—handling geometry operations, coordinate transformations, and file reading and writing—behind a Pythonic interface. Over its ten-year history, GeoPandas has evolved from a single package to a cornerstone of geospatial analysis in Python, anchoring a broader ecosystem of tools. Thousands of downstream projects rely upon GeoPandas, spanning scientific fields from Earth observation and climate modelling to urban analytics and epidemiology. This article provides an overview of the package's history, design, social and technical infrastructure, and future plans. By making spatial analysis more accessible with a standard open-source toolset, GeoPandas democratises access to spatial analysis, facilitates reproducibility, and accelerates scientific discovery.
keywords: Data structures; GIS; python; Software; Spatial analysis; Vector geometry

abstract: Accurate building function mapping is vital for urban analytics, yet existing methods often rely on costly labels and struggle with mixed-function complexity. This study develops an integrated framework that combines street view images (SVIs) with foundation models to achieve scalable and fine-grained building function analysis. Specifically, the GroundingDINO+SAM method detects and segments building facades, and the CLIP model identifies fine-grained building function via zero-shot prompting. A façade segmentation method then quantifies mixed-function intensity, and a cognitive alignment module evaluates the consistency between model attention and human reasoning. We validated the framework using a large corpus of SVIs from Shenzhen, China, covering diverse building types and functions. Results show that our framework achieves an overall classification accuracy of 74.25%. It also captures mixed-function patterns and intra-building functional diversity, offering insights beyond conventional methods. Human-model cognitive alignment shows both consistency and divergence, with visual, semantic, and overall scores of 0.14, 0.48, and 0.63. Interpretability analysis indicates that humans focus on symbolic cues, whereas foundation models emphasize textures, geometry, and context. These findings provide methodological and practical insights for future urban analytics and city management.
keywords: Building function; CLIP; Foundation models; Street view image; Zero-shot

abstract: Street view imagery (SVI) is now widely used to assess urban living environments, yet cross-platform differences in sensors, viewing geometry, and image quality continue to limit data integration. Using paired Baidu Street View (BSV) and Google Street View (GSV) images from Hong Kong, we propose a dual-scale framework to test whether physical streetscape structure and model-derived perception remain comparable across platforms. The framework combines stacking ensemble learning, SHAP-based interpretation, and Mantel correlation analysis at both sampling-point and pixel scales. At the sampling-point scale, vegetation, buildings, and sky show strong BSV-GSV agreement, with correlations of 0.753, 0.756, and 0.720, respectively. Perceptual dimensions also show moderate-to-high consistency, ranging from 0.591 for “Depressing” to 0.672 for “Safe.” At the pixel scale, simulated vegetation distributions are highly consistent, with an average correlation of 0.84 and more than 98% of the study area significant at p < 0.001; “Beauty” also maintains a positive correlation of 0.645. Further structural and causal analyses suggest that natural elements tend to enhance perceived beauty, whereas artificial and traffic-related features are generally linked to negative perceptual effects. Robustness tests using SegFormer and DeepLabv3+ under ADE20K and Cityscapes, together with perception-backbone tests using ResNet50 and CLIP, indicate that the main structural consistency findings are stable across segmentation pipelines, while perceptual consistency remains more sensitive to the selected backbone. Overall, this study offers a robust methodological foundation for urban design and sustainable city assessment by improving spatial prediction accuracy and interpretability.
keywords: ADE20k; Baidu; Google; MIT place pulse 2.0; Street view image; VGG-16

abstract: Driven by the synergistic intensification of global climate change and rapid urbanization, Emergency Medical Services (EMS) demand in megacities is increasingly sensitive to environmental fluctuations. However, existing studies often rely on aggregated data at coarse spatial scales, masking intra-urban heterogeneity and micro-scale risk patterns. This study developed a high-resolution spatiotemporal analysis framework by integrating 379,382 EMS dispatch records from Beijing (2017–2018) into a 1 km * 1 km grid. We employed a Tweedie-distribution-based XGBoost machine learning model combined with SHAP framework to quantify non-linear effects, time-lag dynamics, and spatial heterogeneity of environmental drivers. The model effectively explained over 82% of spatiotemporal variation in EMS demand (R2 = 0.8211). Mean temperature exhibited a U-shaped association with EMS demand, with high temperatures (>25 °C) exerting stronger effects than low temperatures (<0 °C). Both cold waves and heatwaves exhibited significant time-lag effects, with risk intensity peaking at lag week 2. Spatially, heatwaves and cold waves present distinct risk zones across different lag periods, with the most severely impacted areas concentrated primarily in the urban core and the central districts of suburban areas. These findings underscore the necessity of micro-scale risk identification for building climate-resilient EMS systems. We recommend implementing 1 km grid-based early warning systems and maintaining 2-week enhanced monitoring windows following extreme weather events, alongside targeted interventions for vulnerable populations within the identified “risk patches.”
keywords: Cold waves; Emergency medical services (EMS); Heatwaves; Machine learning; Megacity resilience; Spatiotemporal heterogeneity

abstract: City2Graph is an open-source Python library that streamlines workflows for heterogeneous Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in urban systems. Cities are complex systems of diverse spatial relations long modelled as graphs in network science, and recent advances in GNNs have further enabled the identification of non-linear patterns of urban complexity. Unlike homogeneous graphs with a single node and edge type, heterogeneous graphs with multiple types are receiving growing attention to accommodate richer information in GNNs. However, their diffusion remains constrained by fragmented graph construction processes across different data domains, and by the lack of a unified framework for converting constructed graphs into GNN-ready tensors. City2Graph standardises graph construction across domains of morphology, transportation, mobility, and proximity. The library supports conversions between spatial geometries, network topologies, and tensors for spatial analysis with visualisation, network analysis, and GNN training, respectively. City2Graph also supports metapath construction, capturing higher-order connections across node and edge types (e.g., areas linked via multimodal transit). The library's efficacy was demonstrated through a case study on clustering urban functions in Liverpool, UK, using Graph Autoencoder models with three relation types: spatial contiguity, walk-based accessibility, and multimodal accessibility between census units. Compared with the homogeneous model, heterogeneous models identified spatially coherent clusters that aligned more closely with defined accessibility patterns. City2Graph enables reproducible workflows for heterogeneous GNNs and model interpretation, fostering comprehensive understanding of urban systems across disciplines. The library is released under the BSD 3-Clause License on GitHub.
keywords: 15-minute accessibility; Geospatial artificial intelligence; Graph representation learning; Multimodal transportation; Open source software; Overture Maps; Urban morphology

abstract: Social media offers vital near real-time data for flood response, yet extracting accurate geospatial information from unstructured texts remains a significant challenge. The emergence of large language models (LLMs) presents new opportunities to address this task. This study systematically evaluates the spatial reasoning capabilities of LLMs within disaster contexts. We introduce FloodLoc-Four, a hierarchical framework comprising four tasks: disaster-related information validity classification, location span extraction, spatial semantic classification, and standardized address generation. Additionally, a bilingual benchmark dataset, FloodLang, was developed covering Chinese and English flood social media texts. Experiments indicate that Gemini 2.5-Pro and GPT-5 achieve the best overall performance, showing clear advantages in English across all tasks, particularly in location span extraction and standardized address generation. In contrast, the DeepSeek series exhibits more balanced performance between Chinese and English, with relatively small cross-lingual gaps across task levels. While Qwen and Llama exhibit limited cross-lingual stability. These results delineate the practical capability boundaries of current LLMs and offer guidance for selecting models in multilingual flood emergency applications.
keywords: Benchmarking framework; Disaster dataset; Flood disaster; Geoinformation extraction; Large language models

abstract: Urban villages (UVs) are distinctive informal settlements formed during China's rapid urbanization. These settlements are characterized by high-density buildings, mixed functions, and complex street layouts, currently accommodating nearly one-quarter of the urban population in cities across developing regions. While the influence of street environmental characteristics on residents' walking behavior has been well documented, their application in microscale environments of informal settlements has been rarely explored. Moreover, previous studies have primarily relied on traditional methods such as questionnaire surveys and GPS tracking, neglecting high-frequency real-time pedestrian trajectory tracking, which may lead to incomplete understanding of environment-behavior relationships. To address these research gaps, we employed Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) remote sensing technology combined with deep learning algorithms to trace pedestrian spatiotemporal behavior patterns across four street typologies in a Shenzhen UV. We extracted functional features and human-scale visual features from street view imagery, then employed machine learning models to analyze their influence mechanisms on pedestrian flow. Our findings suggest that, in the observed daytime UV settings, functional accessibility variables showed stronger predictive associations with pedestrian flow than objective visual/morphological variables, and this influence mechanism exhibits strong spatial dependency across street types. Moreover, certain functional attributes demonstrate consistent dominant effects, while spatial interventions show contrasting impacts depending on street width and capacity. Cross-regional analysis across 43 UVs suggests that the visual-feature extraction framework is scalable across diverse UV contexts, while full functional-behavioral validation remains future work. These insights question current regeneration practices focused on appearance-oriented physical upgrading and suggest prioritizing functional accessibility enhancements, offering evidence-based guidance for informal settlement upgrading across broader geographic scopes in cities within emerging economies.
keywords: Deep learning; Pedestrian flow; Street typology; UAV remote sensing; Urban villages

abstract: Digitalisation has transformed public transport services worldwide, yet disparities in access, skills, and outcomes continue to reinforce a digital divide in how citizens engage with these services. While previous studies have examined the digital divide in internet use and smart technologies, few have explored how these inequalities manifest in everyday interactions with digital public transport platforms, extending to citizen participation in government-provided digital services. To this end, we investigated user experiences of public transport applications in Birmingham, whose digital inclusion is disproportionate to its status as a major urban and economic hub in the UK, by analysing 4275 user reviews on public transport services collected from the Apple App Store and Google Play Store between 2016 and 2025. Using a mixed natural language processing (NLP) approach combining topic modelling and sentiment analysis, we identified key themes and emotional tones in user feedback. Results revealed three dominant topics: App Performance, Usability, and Service Satisfaction, each conceptually aligned with the access, ability, and motivation dimensions of the digital divide theory. Sentiment analysis showed generally negative evaluations, particularly around technical access barriers and satisfaction issues. By integrating user-generated data with digital divide theory, these results provide novel empirical evidence of how inequalities in digital engagement persist within digital twin planning and smart city transport systems and highlight the importance of inclusive digital design for equitable and sustainable mobility access.
keywords: Artificial intelligence; Digital divide; Inclusive planning; Natural language processing; Public transport; Smart City

abstract: The built environment shapes everyday social encounters, yet existing research often relies on linear effects and overlooks contextual heterogeneity. This study investigates how multi-scale built environment features of 15-min community life circles influence social encounter opportunities in Chengdu, China. We construct an Encounter Opportunity Index (EOI) from anonymized GPS dwell trajectories of 7,480,793 users to quantify potential copresence intensity in open public settings. A total of 18,856 network-constrained life circles are delineated, and 21 built environment and control variables spanning place-level perceptual quality, block-level functional structure, and community-level accessibility are assembled from street view imagery, points of interest, building footprints, remote sensing, and road networks. A Geographical XGBoost model (R2 = 0.862) trained with spatially blocked cross-validation is coupled with SHAP decomposition to reveal nonlinear response patterns. K-means clustering classifies life circles into three socio-spatial types for stratified analysis. Results identify three dominant nonlinear patterns: threshold-plateau responses in pedestrian infrastructure and transit density, persistent negative associations between green coverage and encounter opportunities, and staged escalation effects in spatial overlap and floor area ratio. Stratified SHAP analysis reveals pronounced contextual dependency: peripheral life circles are most sensitive to infrastructure deficit compensation, middle-ring life circles respond to green environment quality and pedestrian safety, and core life circles are shaped by spatial agglomeration and streetscape quality. These findings advance the understanding of nonlinear, context-contingent pathways through which the built environment structures encounter opportunities, offering differentiated planning guidance for community life circle optimization.
keywords: Built environment; Community life circle; Encounter opportunity; Explainable machine learning; GPS trajectory; Nonlinear effects

abstract: Population growth and economic vitality in Metro Vancouver increasingly depend on immigration, as natural population growth is projected to stagnate by 2035. Residential segregation patterns emerge from complex interactions between individual preferences, socio-demographic characteristics, and urban spatial structure. This study develops a geospatial agent-based model to simulate settlement dynamics of immigrants who arrived between 2016 and 2021 in Metro Vancouver, comparing two classification scenarios: a broad ethnic diversity scheme and a more finely resolved origins diversity scheme. Model performance was evaluated using the Simpson's Diversity Index (SDI) and error metrics (MAE, MSE, RMSE), while kernel density analysis (KDA) was primarily applied on an ethnic basis to identify where different ethnic groups concentrated spatially. Results indicated that the origins diversity scenario more accurately reproduces primary settlement hubs, captures population heterogeneity, and aligns with observed Census patterns, outperforming the ethnic diversity scenario with lower errors (MAE = 0.210, MSE = 0.063, RMSE = 0.251). Nonetheless, secondary, dispersed, and minority clusters remain underrepresented, highlighting the challenge of modeling smaller and peripheral populations. Besides, sensitivity analysis and model calibration indicated that settlement outcomes are influenced by both social preferences and spatial accessibility, with social affinity playing the more dominant role. These findings underscore the utility of ABMs for understanding urban settlement dynamics, guiding planning strategies, and supporting policy interventions, while emphasizing the need for methodological refinements to better capture minority populations and fine-scale spatial patterns. The study provides actionable insights to inform equitable, inclusive, and sustainable urban development aligned with Metro 2050.
keywords: Agent-based modeling (ABM); Complex systems; Geographic information systems (GIS); Immigrant settlement; Residential segregation; Spatial diversity

abstract: Building height is a critical but largely underrepresented element of 3D geospatial information. Existing height estimation methods often rely on expensive equipment or labor-intensive data collection, which restricts their scalability and practical deployment in large-scale scenarios. Although abundant sensors such as cameras and global navigation satellite system (GNSS) chips embedded in smartphones offer a low-cost alternative solution for retrieving building height information, these approaches typically require extensive manual intervention. To address these challenges, this article presents a joint building height estimation and pose optimization method using single-view smartphone image, leveraging widely available 2D building footprints. The proposed approach utilizes visual geometric features to identify building corner points and assign associated confidence scores. Building height and smartphone pose are then jointly estimated by minimizing the confidence-weighted reprojection errors between the 3D corner points and their corresponding image observations. Numerous experiments on 50 diverse real-world buildings demonstrate that the proposed method, with fully automated processing, achieves a mean absolute error of 0.70 m and a relative error of 3.47% in height estimation, outperforming both existing smartphone-based methods and street-view image-based methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency. The joint optimization scheme yields an improvement of 22.7% in absolute building height estimation accuracy over existing pose-only optimization. Furthermore, the average horizontal positioning error is significantly reduced from 10.0 m, based on initial GNSS chip results, to 1.8 m. These results highlight the method's potential as a lightweight and scalable solution for Level-of-Detail 1 3D building modeling and robust smartphone localization in real-world urban environments using only low-cost consumer devices.
keywords: 3D building model; Building height estimation; Pose optimization; Single image; Smartphone localization

abstract: Probabilistic space-time prisms (PSTPs) are used to measure probabilities of location for individuals over time. Intersecting PSTPs for different individuals enables probabilities of co-location and proximity to be computed for each voxel, or volume element, that represents a time step for a specific location. This paper extends PSTP analysis by developing an approach to test the statistical significance of the calculated co-location and proximity measures. First, PSTPs were generated for 20 individual Mallard and Muscovy ducks tracked simultaneously. Second, the PSTPs were used to calculate probabilities of co-location and proximity for all 190 possible dyads. Third, species-specific agent-based models (ABMs) and a generic random walk model (RWM) were developed as null models to simulate tracking data over the same tracking duration, with 1000 replicates used to generate confidence intervals for each dyad. Finally, 95% confidence intervals for co-location and proximity obtained from the PSTP analysis were compared to 95% confidence intervals for co-location and proximity derived from the 1000 replicates of ABMs and RWM to evaluate if dyads were interacting more than, less than, or as expected under the null models. The results showed differences in co-location and proximity between dyads, but most importantly, the significance of those interactions was highly dependent on the null model used for comparison. The RWM typically predicted fewer co-locations and larger proximities in comparison to the species-specific ABMs, often yielding different conclusions about the direction and strength of interactions. The findings suggest that the significance of intra-and inter-species interactions should be evaluated in the context of the species' habitat and movement preferences through ABMs.
keywords: Agent-based model; Inter-species interaction; Interaction; Probabilistic space-time prisms; Random walk model; Space-time analysis; Time geography

abstract: Urban informal settlements in China are often characterized by high building and population densities, narrow alleys, and intricate road networks. These features present significant safety challenges and complicate evacuation planning due to their high vulnerability to disasters and the difficulty of large-scale reconstruction. To address these challenges, we propose a coupled simulation–optimization framework designed to evaluate and enhance the road-network performance in these dense informal settlements, thereby improving their disaster-evacuation resilience. By integrating geographic information system (GIS)-based environmental reconstruction, potential-field navigation, and a Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH)-based crowd density and movement model, the framework models pedestrian dynamics. The movement model is calibrated and validated against empirical corridor-level fundamental-diagram data, while paired multi-seed village-scale simulations and plausibility checks are used to examine the consistency of the resulting evacuation patterns. A multi-objective optimization algorithm is then used to identify nondominated micro-regeneration strategies that balance evacuation efficiency with reconstruction cost. A case study conducted in Shipai Village, a dense informal settlement in Guangzhou, China, demonstrates that this approach effectively pinpoints critical network bottlenecks. The representative intervention yields substantial improvements in evacuation metrics while requiring only localized road widening. Sensitivity analyses of crowd-model and optimization parameters further show the robustness of the evacuation performance and intervention selection. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method and the findings offer practical and cost-effective guidance for urban planners seeking to improve the resilience and safety of urban informal settlements. The code is available at https://github.com/rui-research/roadnet-evac-opt.
keywords: Crowd simulation; Disaster response; Informal settlements; Multi-objective optimization; Sustainable Development Goal 11 (SDG 11); Urban regeneration

abstract: Border effects suppress cross-boundary flows of people and goods, and it is precisely this suppression that drives the gradual divergence of built environment and socioeconomic conditions on either side of a boundary. Measuring border effects from flows is therefore more proximate to the border effect itself than inferring them from downstream outcomes such as housing price differentials or service provision gaps. To address the challenge that flow-based border effects are inherently unobservable and thus unable to be systematically characterized, this study proposes a representation-explanation framework. In the representation stage, a flow-based geographically weighted additive gravity model (FB-GWAGM) that treats each border crossing as an additive increment to physical distance is adopted. In the explanation stage, reliability-weighted random forest models with SHapley Additive exPlanations analysis identify the built environment and socioeconomic factors affecting border thickness. On the basis of the modeling results, the spatial heterogeneity of border thickness is identified and quantified in distance-equivalent units, and the contributions of built environment and socioeconomic factors to this heterogeneity are decomposed in the same metric, enabling direct comparison across border types and factor dimensions. These findings demonstrate that the representation-explanation framework provides a replicable and physically interpretable approach to quantifying flow-based border effects, advancing the understanding of how borders shape spatial interaction within cities and revealing the socioeconomically contingent nature of border thickness heterogeneity.
keywords: Border effect; Geographically weighted additive gravity model; Intra-urban commuting; Representation-explanation framework

abstract: Managing municipal solid waste in rapidly urbanizing Sub-Saharan Africa remains challenging due to dispersed informal dumping and limited high-resolution datasets for spatial monitoring. We present an open-access deep learning model for automated detection of openly dumped dispersed MSW (ODD-MSW) via crowdsourced UAV imagery, trained and evaluated across 29 regions in 10 Sub-Saharan African countries, encompassing diverse environmental contexts. A deep learning model trained on manually annotated image tiles achieved an overall accuracy of 92.87% (F1 = 0.927) in detecting ODD-MSW across all study regions. Applied without any site-specific retraining to 25 independent OpenAerialMap scenes from 21 cities in 19 countries on five continents, the frozen model retained an F1 score of 0.867, providing direct evidence of transferability beyond the training domain. Predicted distributions reveal heterogeneous accumulation patterns, ranging from localized hotspots — often along waterways, where waste can exacerbate flood and public health risks — to more dispersed litter across urban areas. Waste accumulation is most strongly associated with population density (Spearman ρ = 0.674, p<0.001) and indicators of lack of local infrastructure access (ρ = 0.700, p<0.001), whereas its relationship with broader measures of regional development is weaker and not statistically significant (ρ = 0.215, p=0.26), highlighting the importance of fine-scale data for understanding localized waste dynamics. By releasing the model, this study provides a ready-to-use tool for UAV imagery collected by municipalities and local mapping communities, enabling ODD-MSW monitoring without extensive technical expertise. This approach empowers local practitioners to convert UAV imagery into actionable insights, supporting targeted interventions and improved municipal solid waste management across Sub-Saharan Africa.
keywords: Computer vision; Crowdsourced UAV imagery; Municipal solid waste; Open dumping; OpenAerialMap; Sub-Saharan Africa

abstract: As the COVID-19 pandemic recedes, urban life, economic activities, and transportation systems appear to have returned to normal. Yet latent post-pandemic impacts on shifts in socioeconomic stratification within human mobility remain under-explored. Using large-scale longitudinal mobile signaling data for nearly 8 million residents in Beijing between 2019 and 2024, weighted using census data and integrated with social attributes and housing price data, this study examines how socioeconomic stratification patterns and mobility behaviors evolve across socioeconomic groups. Here, we show that the potential stratification has intensified in the post-pandemic era. First, the place-level and inter-group contact-based socioeconomic stratification index increased by 34.83% and 32.34%, respectively. Counterfactual simulations reveal that shortened travel distances and homogeneous mobility preferences reduced opportunities for cross-group encounters. Second, residential proximity and shared social attributes significantly explain variations in opportunities for inter-group co-presence. Spatial disparities in urban infrastructure configuration can either mitigate or reinforce mobility-related socioeconomic stratification across locations. Collectively, this study underscores that spatial context, socioeconomic characteristics, and behavioral preferences shape mobility stratification, offering empirical evidence for understanding post-pandemic socioeconomic stratification dynamics.
keywords: Beijing; Mobile signaling data; Social stratification; Socio-spatial relations; Urban mobility

abstract: As cities expand both outward and upward, assessing global urbanization requires a three-dimensional perspective that captures the complete picture of urban growth. However, conventional land-consumption metrics fail to capture vertical intensification, while large-scale building-volume data that are consistent across years in data source, method, resolution, and precision remain difficult to obtain. To address this gap, this study asks whether population potential, inferred from remotely sensed physical environments, can serve as a scalable proxy for building volume and reveal urban expansion patterns that remain hidden in 2D assessments. Using fifteen East Asian megacity regions as a comparative sample, we integrate gridded population potential, land consumption rate, height change rate, space consumption rate, and district-level development indicators within an urban scaling framework. The results show that population potential explains building volume more effectively than population count, increasing the mean R2 of the scaling model from 0.4891 to 0.6432 when using population potential. Development-mode analysis further reveals scale-dependent patterns: across megacity regions, vertical growth differentiates national urban systems more clearly than horizontal expansion, whereas within megacity regions, more developed districts generally expand less horizontally and often grow more vertically. Finally, the comparison between LCRPGR and SCRPGR shows that many districts appearing coordinated under the 2D land-consumption assessment still exhibit rapid volumetric growth relative to population growth. These findings suggest that population potential and volumetric diagnostics can complement conventional SDG 11.3.1 indicators by revealing dimensions of urban expansion that are overlooked in two-dimensional land-use assessment.
keywords: Building volume; Dasymetric mapping; East Asia; Land use efficiency; Sustainable development goals; Urban scaling law

abstract: Urban development is increasingly shifting from outward expansion toward the renewal and optimization of existing urban areas. This transition has created a growing demand for building layout generation methods that can satisfy complex planning requirements while maintaining sound spatial organization. However, most existing end-to-end approaches jointly model building attributes, morphology, and spatial arrangement. This unified process makes it difficult to trace how planning requirements affect spatial outcomes, inspect intermediate decisions, or adjust generated scenarios. This study proposes HyperLayout, a decoupled and planning-oriented framework for parcel-level building layout generation. Rather than treating layout generation as a single synthesis task, HyperLayout organizes it into three interpretable stages: development-capacity configuration, building form generation, and spatial layout optimization. Through explicit constraint propagation, parcel-level planning objectives are progressively converted into building attributes, geometric conditions, and spatial optimization criteria. This structure makes intermediate decisions and outputs easier to inspect and revise throughout the generation process. Experiments show that HyperLayout improves upon the evaluated baselines in both building form generation and building layout optimization. The framework produces layouts with improved geometric consistency, spatial organization, adaptation to parcel boundaries, and compliance with planning constraints. It also supports the controlled exploration of alternative scenarios under different planning objectives at parcel and community scales. These findings suggest that workflow decomposition and explicit constraint propagation provide a practical framework for developing interpretable and controllable AI-assisted planning tools for urban design and redevelopment.
keywords: Building layout generation; Controllable generation; Decoupled framework; Multi-agent reinforcement learning; Planning constraints

abstract: Digital planning for urban systems can benefit from integrated frameworks that capture cross-sectoral dependencies, impact assessment, support causal reasoning, and adapt to diverse data sources. We present a methodological approach for Digital Twinning that combines backward-chaining analysis with Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) to identify, decompose, and interlink key performance indicators across three critical planning domains: drinking water supply, urban heat stress, and housing provision. Building on a comprehensive indicator review, we selected key targets and traced each to its fundamental components using the DPSIR framework (Driving Forces, Pressures, States, Impacts, Responses). We quantified relational dependencies and network centrality metrics to construct sector-specific DAGs, then merged overlapping elements into an integrated cross-sector model, revealing critical causal pathways. This enables scenario testing across diverse drivers, including climate change, demographic shifts, and credit conditions. Our results demonstrate how infrastructural and natural system interventions propagate through water reliability, thermal comfort, and housing affordability. The framework clarifies data requirements and analytic workflows for Digital Planning tools while offering a scalable template for cross-sectoral impact analysis. By structuring complex interactions into a unified causal schema, planners can use this approach to evaluate trade-offs and derive evidence for decision-making.
keywords: Causal reasoning; Digital Twins; Evidence-based planning; Planning support systems; Strategic urban planning

abstract: Human mobility analysis increasingly relies on large-scale trajectory data, yet results remain highly sensitive to preprocessing choices that are rarely applied in a consistent or well-documented manner. Stop detection, which transforms raw location traces into sequences of visited places, is a particularly critical and bias-prone step, with parameter choices often guided by dataset-specific conventions. The absence of systematic and transparent parameter-selection practices risks introducing methodological bias and limits the comparability and reproducibility of mobility studies. Here, we introduce OptimalStop, a model-agnostic optimisation framework for stop detection that exploits a predictability–complexity trade-off in human mobility trajectories to guide preprocessing. OptimalStop operates as a higher-level tuning layer applicable to any method that produces symbolic mobility sequences. By framing stop detection as a multi-objective optimisation problem, the framework identifies compact Pareto-optimal sets of parameter configurations that balance predictability and structural complexity, avoiding over-fragmented or over-aggregated representations. We evaluate OptimalStop on both real-world and synthetic mobility datasets using multiple stop detection algorithms, and confirm through controlled synthetic experiments that the predictability–complexity trade-off is structurally grounded in recurrent return-to-place behaviour rather than being a mathematical artefact of discretisation. The results show that OptimalStop consistently retains near-optimal solutions while substantially reducing the effective parameter search space within a reasonable computational time. An optional automatic selection strategy further demonstrates that high-quality stop detection can be obtained without ground truth, outperforming or matching commonly used sensitivity-based tuning approaches. We release OptimalStop under an open licence, providing a transparent and reproducible framework for parameter selection that supports more structured mobility data preprocessing. While demonstrated here for stop detection, the underlying predictability–complexity balance offers a general perspective for mitigating methodological bias in mobility analytics.
keywords: Entropy; Human mobility; Predictability; Stop detection; Stop location; Trajectory analysis; Urban analytics

abstract: Urban vitality is a key quality of the livability and attractiveness of a city, with street-level social dynamics recognized as a central representation. However, existing approaches to capturing such dynamics, primarily through pedestrian volume, rely on static imagery, location-based proxies, or custom sensors. Such methods are typically discontinuous, limited in spatio-temporal resolution, costly, and overlook the role of sound in shaping environments. To address these gaps, this study explores the feasibility of using Street View Video (SVV), a novel, promising, yet under-utilized data source, for capturing street-level dynamics. Leveraging widely available crowdsourced city tour videos as a representative form of SVV, we develop an automated and scalable framework for high-precision geo-localization of SVV by extracting textual and depth information. Further, we propose a visual–auditory pipeline that integrates continuous pedestrian activity and sound environments as complementary dimensions that reveal street-level social dynamics. Using Melbourne as a case study, we identified 892 high-quality and geolocatable videos totaling over 542 h and achieved an accuracy of 77% for geo-localization. We generated spatio-temporal maps that not only reproduced well-studied pedestrian volume patterns, but also previously neglected aspects, including human actions (walking, standing, sitting), sound intensity, and sound types (speech, music, vehicle). Correlation and quadrant analyses further explored the relationships among these vitality dimensions, revealing distinctive street characteristics and highlighting the limitations of conventional road classifications. Overall, these findings demonstrate the potential of SVV as a multimodal and reproducible source of urban vitality indicators, providing a proof-of-concept for future urban sensing applications.
keywords: Built environment; Computer vision; Urban analytics; Urban vibrancy; Virtual tour; Volunteered geographic information

abstract: Urban tree canopy coverage (TCC) targets are increasingly used for heat mitigation. However, translating fixed percentage targets into context-specific cooling benefits, population coverage across cooling thresholds, and spatial priorities is essential for making them actionable in planning practice. This study develops a spatially explicit framework that couples a Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based land surface temperature (LST) surrogate model with multi-objective optimization to evaluate TCC increment scenarios in residential areas. Using Shanghai, China, as a case study, we first show that incorporating neighbourhood context improves LST prediction, with the GraphSAGE model consistently outperforming non-spatial machine-learning models. We then compare a uniform 30% TCC baseline with three equality-oriented scenarios using population-weighted, heat-exposure-weighted and vulnerability-weighted perspectives. With mean summer LST as the baseline, the equality-oriented knee solutions required 18.0–20.2% more canopy investment than the uniform baseline while increasing mean LST reduction by 45.3–48.8%. The three equality-oriented scenarios produced similar city-scale cooling patterns but led to different local canopy-allocation priorities. Marginal cooling gains diminished as added TCC increased, with the most rapid gains occurring within the first 20 percentage points of TCC increment, bringing average TCC close to the 30% benchmark in Shanghai. At a 20-percentage-point TCC increment, about 65% of the population achieved at least 1 °C LST reduction, whereas stronger cooling thresholds remained difficult to reach even under high-budget scenarios. Overall, this study translates fixed-percentage canopy targets into budget-sensitive cooling outcomes, equality responses and spatial priorities, providing an urban-scale screening framework for TCC planning.
keywords: Cooling-benefit equality; Graph neural network; Multi-objective optimization; Tree canopy coverage; Urban greening planning

abstract: Small-area population forecasting has become increasingly critical for establishing localized policies to address regional demographic disparities. Due to its minimal data requirements and methodological simplicity, trend extrapolation offers a practical approach given the limited availability of detailed demographic data. The Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model enhances this approach by effectively capturing complex non-linear temporal dependencies. However, forecasting accuracy is often limited by ignoring spatial interdependence, as demographic shifts are frequently driven by interactions between neighboring areas rather than occurring independently within each area. This study evaluates the impact of integrating spatio-temporal neighboring population dynamics into a deep learning model for small-area population forecasting. Specifically, it compares a proposed Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)-LSTM model, which integrates interregional population changes by employing one-dimensional convolutional layer as spatial feature extractor for neighboring dynamics, against the standard LSTM model that treats each unit as an isolated series. The results demonstrate that the CNN-LSTM model generally outperforms the standard LSTM model in overall global accuracy, primarily driven by its performance in areas with high spatial association. This advantage is particularly evident in areas with low temporal but high spatial association, where information from neighbors compensates for discontinuous historical trends. In contrast, caution is required when applying the CNN-LSTM in areas characterized by high temporal and low spatial association, as uncorrelated spatial information from neighbors could act as noise over long-term forecasting.
keywords: CNN-LSTM; Deep learning; LSTM; Small-area population forecasting; Trend extrapolation

abstract: In the context of a circular economy, the built environment can be regarded as a reservoir of future recoverable resources. Early identification of buildings at risk of demolition enables targeted reuse and recycling strategies, contributing to global warming mitigation and waste avoidance. Most existing studies rely on spatially explicit analyses and lifetime distribution functions for demolition forecasting, yet do not comprehensively account for the multiple interacting drivers influencing demolition at the building level. This study proposes a spatiotemporal machine learning framework for modelling building demolition risk across large geographic areas. A consolidated dataset is constructed by integrating Geographical Information System (GIS)-based spatial data with building characteristics, surrounding built environment attributes, local demolition dynamics, and statistical socioeconomic indicators. Using this dataset, several machine learning models are employed and evaluated for predicting demolition events and estimating building-level risk scores across Switzerland over different time horizons. Extreme class imbalance is identified as a major challenge, and several strategies are evaluated to address this issue. Model performance is evaluated based on ranking capability and effectiveness in identifying high-risk buildings. The results demonstrate strong performance despite the low base rate of demolition events, with the models effectively prioritising buildings at elevated risk. To enhance interpretability, this study applies Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) to quantify the contribution of different features to model predictions. The findings provide insights into the key drivers of demolition, supporting data-driven decision-making for urban planners and policymakers. This study advances the development of data-driven tools for sustainable urban planning and establishes a benchmark for building-level demolition prediction.
keywords: Building demolition risk; Building stock modelling; Class imbalance; Spatiotemporal machine learning; Urban mining

abstract: The 15-min city concept promises equitable access to essential services through walkable neighborhoods, yet traditional accessibility assessments fail to capture the dynamic impact of vehicular exposure on pedestrian experiences. This study introduces a novel computational framework that measures near-real-time, path-specific vehicular exposure during individual walking journeys by integrating large-scale mobility datasets including mobile phone trajectories (approximately 50% population coverage), GPS data from heavy trucks (75% coverage), and comprehensive public transit schedules in Beijing, China. We develop multi-scale exposure indices that distinguish between cars, trucks, and buses at road, location, and individual trip levels, revealing systematic inequities across socioeconomic groups: higher-income groups face intense car risks in amenity-rich urban areas, while lower-income groups are disproportionately burdened by truck traffic. Critically, we model an access gap that quantifies how traffic avoidance behavior constrains walkable access, revealing that vehicular exposure creates invisible barriers that systematically reduce the practical reach of the 15-min city. These findings compel a reinterpretation of walkability—from mere proximity to an experiential quality—and provide essential insights to identify and mitigate the environmental injustices that undermine equitable urban design.
keywords: 15-min city; environmental justice; urban accessibility; vehicular exposure; walkability

abstract: Characterising and classifying urban functions is a long-standing research focus in urban studies and plays a critical role in urban management and community renewal. However, traditional point-of-interest (POI) categories rely on predefined labels that are often inconsistent across cities and may not fully capture how places are described, represented, or experienced in user-generated data. Further, point-based representations are highly sensitive to spatial aggregation scales, which limits their ability to capture areal functional characteristics and relative differences in POI activity intensity. To address these challenges, we propose a unified framework that, for the first time, leverages place reviews from Google Maps, a form of user-generated geographic information, as a previously untapped POI-linked extended data stream for urban functional inference and classification. Specifically, we employ pre-trained BERT and Vision Transformer models to embed textual and visual information from place reviews, enabling POIs in Singapore and Hong Kong to be represented and clustered within a shared functional embedding space. We then incorporate the weighted volume of place reviews as an indicator of relative POI activity intensity to construct category intensity vectors for spatial units, and demonstrate their effectiveness through cross-city similarity matching tasks. Finally, urban functional classification is conducted across three spatial scales: a 1 km hexagonal grid, administrative areas, and traffic analysis zones (TAZs), using graph neural networks combined with k-means clustering, producing results that preserve spatial continuity and robustness. The proposed framework provides a data-driven approach that highlights the value of place reviews as a complementary data source to conventional POIs and offers a reliable urban functional classification that works across different cities.
keywords: Graph neural networks; Multimodal representation learning; Urban functional classification; Volunteered geographic information (VGI)

abstract: Covering location problems have received considerable attention in spatial optimization, exemplified by applications such as urban security monitoring. While current optimization techniques are effective at small to moderate scales, advances in multi-source spatial big data and geospatial analytics toolkit compel us to address spatially large problems. Unlike traditional approaches relying on coarse demand aggregation, these fine-grained spatial problems involve millions to tens of millions of demand points. In this paper, we focus on a general backup covering location problem involving heterogeneous, anisotropic devices in a 3-D environment. Recognizing that this NP-hard problem becomes computationally intractable at such scales, we exploit the spatial features and supply–demand relationships to develop efficient, problem-specific spatial reduction strategies, collectively referred to as presolving. These strategies drastically reduce the number of decision variables and constraints while preserving optimality. Extensive computational experiments demonstrate theoretical rigor and practical viability on synthetic problem instances and a real world case study in Beijing, China. Thanks to the proposed presolving techniques, optimal solutions can be obtained rapidly for these instances involving up to 20 million demand points, which are previously considered unsolvable.
keywords: Backup coverage; Facility location; Presolving; Security monitoring; Spatial optimization

abstract: Private cars generate substantial urban health, environmental, and social costs. Despite their continued dominance and extensive subsidization, cities are increasingly experimenting with measures to reduce private car use. In 2023, a residential neighborhood in Berlin repurposed approximately 350 on–street parking spaces – about 13% of the area's total – by converting them into green spaces, outdoor classrooms, shared–mobility stations for e–bikes and e–scooters, and designated zones for deliveries and local businesses. The intervention was evaluated using a controlled before–after quasi–experimental design, based on surveys conducted shortly before implementation and six months afterward. The research design distinguishes between a main and a secondary treatment area, two demographically and socioeconomically comparable control areas, and two adjacent neighborhoods potentially affected by traffic and parking displacement. More than 11,000 residents were invited to participate in each survey wave. Treatment areas were fully sampled, while residents in control areas were selected through area–based random sampling, yielding effective sample sizes of 2,027 respondents before and 1,770 after the intervention. Difference–in–differences analyses show no significant reduction in private car use among respondents. However, the intervention was associated with improvements in perceived road safety and outdoor physical activity, as well as small reductions in noise annoyance and traffic–related quality–of–life impacts. At the same time, parking search times increased, noise annoyances from visitors and restaurants increased slightly, and adjacent neighborhoods experienced very modest parking displacement. Policy acceptance declined somewhat after implementation but remained positive among a majority of respondents in the wider treatment area, while opinions were more evenly divided among residents living in the main treatment area that was most affected by the intervention. Overall, this study – one of the few quasi–experimental evaluations of parking–space repurposing – highlights both the potential benefits and the trade–offs of neighborhood–level parking-space repurposing.
keywords: Car use reduction; Climate mitigation; Controlled before-after experiment; Germany; Parking-space reduction; Transport intervention; Urban transition experiment

abstract: To support bicycling, cities have focused on providing infrastructure to ensure safe movement. Much less research assesses the provision of adequate bicycle parking, especially residential parking. Because of their higher weight and costs, e-bicycles especially require safe, sheltered and accessible parking. The paper describes the features of home-based bicycle parking for Swiss individuals with and without e-bicycles and assesses variations and discrepancies in residential bicycle parking availability and e-bicycle ownership across land use and household characteristics. The 2021 Swiss Mobility and Transport Microcensus (MTMC) provides a representative national sample of data on e-bicycle ownership and residential bicycle parking (n = 10,154). Variations in logit-based estimated probabilities of e-bicycle ownership and quality parking access across predictor variables are assessed. The probability of having accessible sheltered and secured bicycle parking in a locked room, the golden standard of safety, protection from the elements and ease of use, is low and below that of e-bicycle ownership probabilities, regardless of socio-demographics and location features. Across group characteristics, specific mismatches between parking access and e-bicycle ownership are identified. The largest mismatches are found for homeowners and residents of areas poorly served by public transit. Current housing stock is ill-equipped for parking of e-bicycles, especially in areas where regular cycling is historically low. While existing standards can help shape new housing stock, retrofitting existing residential buildings is an important policy challenge. On street veloboxes may be more feasible. The variety of observed bicycle parking forms also points to the limits of current survey instruments. Improvements to survey instruments are proposed.
keywords: Accessible; Apartments; Cycling; Home; Locked room; Parking; Safety

abstract: Feebates applied to new vehicles are widely used to reduce emissions from the automobile sector, yet most vehicles are traded in second-hand markets. This paper studies how interactions between new and used car markets affect the distributional incidence of a car feebate. Using comprehensive French administrative data on vehicle transactions over the period 2008–2019 and detailed information on used car prices, we develop an accounting framework linking the feebate spillover to vehicle depreciation. We find that over half of the initial feebate is redistributed through used car markets within five years, with important consequences for incidence. Corporate buyers, who face the largest direct tax on new cars, recover approximately two-thirds of their burden through resale and end up close to neutral overall. Among private households, the burden shifts further towards high-income groups, who purchase both more new and more recent used cars. Yet the feebate remains progressive: the net burden as a share of income increases with household income, whether accounting for used car markets or not. These results suggest that the distributional effects of vehicle regulations cannot be assessed on the basis of new car markets alone, and that corporate buyers play a key role in transmitting feebate costs across the car lifecycle.
keywords: Automobile; Corporate vehicles; Distributional effects; Environmental policy; Second-hand markets
