Grounded in the PRECEDE-PROCEED Model and Ecological Systems Theory, we draw on 72 Guangzhou neighborhood surveys to examine how these interactions shape walking duration. Multilevel logistic regression models assess how individual, household, infrastructure, and social environmental factors jointly influence residents’ leisure walking duration, elucidating cross-level interaction mechanisms. Results show that at the individual level, age, number of elderly household members and neighborhood social networks significantly increase leisure walking duration. At the community level, aggregate recreational facility density exerts a significant negative effect on walking duration. Cross-level results showed that longer residential duration buffered the negative associated of street network density on walking via environmental adaptation; neighborhood network facilitated walking only among residents with low avoidance behavior. These patterns delineate the mechanisms of built-environment “adaptation” and social “conditional enablement,” revealing that cross-level interactions between individuals and their environments joint-modulate leisure walking duration.
keywords: Crime safety perception; Interaction; Leisure walking duration; Multi-level model

abstract: Visual, light and thermal conditions in indoor living spaces jointly constitute important environmental characteristics impacting emotional states. Existing studies have mostly examined these environmental characteristics separately, while the pathways through which their combined effects impact emotional states remain insufficiently understood. In this study, a typical indoor space in Chongqing was selected as experimental site. Courtyard landscape, window-to-wall ratio and indoor air temperature were treated as environmental characteristics. Questionnaire data on subjective sensations, comfort evaluations and emotional states were collected from 486 university students. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) was applied to identify the pathways through which environmental characteristics impacted positive valence, negative valence, high arousal, low arousal, stress and fatigue. The results showed that visual conditions significantly impacted emotional states, especially fatigue. Window-to-wall ratio was associated with visual sensation, and its role in positive valence and fatigue was further linked to changes in light sensation. Indoor air temperature mainly impacted positive valence, low arousal and stress through thermal sensation and thermal comfort. Subjective sensations and comfort evaluations formed important mediating pathways linking environmental characteristics to emotional states. Visual conditions increased fatigue when mediated only by visual sensation, but reduced fatigue when visual sensation was further evaluated as comfortable. By distinguishing immediate sensation from subsequent comfort appraisal, this study extends multidomain indoor environment study from identifying environmental effects to explaining how these effects are psychologically translated into different emotional states. These findings are expected to provide a reference for residents’ mental health and emotional state regulation.
keywords: Comfort evaluation; Emotional states; Mediating pathway; Subjective sensation; Visual-light-thermal condition

abstract: Urban built environments may shape children’s mental health and social development, but their combined and potentially nonlinear associations with favourable developmental profiles remain poorly understood. We linked Wave 13 of Understanding Society with multi-source geospatial and street-view data for children aged 8–12 years living in urban areas of England and Wales. The neighbourhood built environment was characterised within 500 m buffers across greenspace, land-use, road-network and service-facility domains. Total Difficulties and Prosocial Behaviour were derived from the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire. XGBoost models with SHAP interpretation were used as an exploratory framework to examine built-environment characteristics associated with Normal-category model outputs, while hierarchical clustering was applied to describe co-occurring environmental configurations. Built-environment characteristics contributed substantially to model interpretation, with greenspace indicators showing prominent contributions and road-network and service-facility characteristics demonstrating outcome-specific nonlinear patterns. Five descriptive neighbourhood typologies were identified, although child-outcome distributions did not differ significantly across clusters. These findings suggest that multidimensional neighbourhood built-environment characteristics may be associated with favourable developmental profiles and highlight the importance of considering environmental configurations and nonlinear relationships in child-friendly urban planning.
keywords: Built Environment; Greenspace; Machine Learning; Mental Health; Nonlinear Analysis; Prosocial Behaviour

abstract: Metro systems influence both land markets and the spatial distribution of accessibility, but these two outcome dimensions do not necessarily move together. This study examines metro station placement in Wuhan from two observable perspectives: parcel-level land-value gradients around metro stations and the distribution of community-level accessibility changes. Using 2,711 land transfers during 2012–2023, pre-construction vacant-land mapping around stations, and a community-level accessibility assessment centered on Metro Line 4, we combine descriptive spatial analysis, hedonic price models, a PSM-DID analysis, and distributional accessibility indicators. The results show that several later metro lines were spatially associated with substantial undeveloped land prior to construction. The hedonic models reveal a negative price-distance gradient in the full Wuhan sample. Within the Line 4 corridor, this gradient remains negative and significant in corridor-wide specifications but becomes statistically insignificant after district fixed effects are introduced, indicating sensitivity to broader spatial heterogeneity. The Line 4-specific PSM-DID estimates are consistently positive across nearest-neighbor, kernel, and caliper matching, indicating a positive post-opening land-price differential within the 1,000-m station area. The accessibility analysis further shows that average potential accessibility improved after Line 4 opened, although the gains remained unevenly distributed across communities. Additional hedonic specifications using the community-level accessibility score suggest that local station proximity and broader network accessibility capture related but distinct dimensions of metro-related land-market outcomes. Overall, the evidence points to a clear land-value gradient around stations and uneven accessibility gains from Line 4.
keywords: Accessibility inequality; Land-value gradients; Metro station placement; Potential accessibility; Wuhan

abstract: Village morphology identification is sensitive to analytical scale, especially where administrative or built-up boundaries aggregate multiple settlement units into a single external form. This issue is particularly relevant to traditional villages, whose internal settlement composition may differ from the morphology expressed by the overall village boundary. This study examines 55 traditional villages in Northeast China and develops a sub-village spatial unit (SVSU)-based multi-scale framework to identify village morphology and diagnose scale mismatch. Six morphology indicators were used to classify SVSU-level morphology into compact, linear, and dispersed types. Village-level morphology was derived by integrating SVSU-level types according to area composition and compared with conventional village-level identification. Scale mismatch was diagnosed for multi-SVSU villages, and diagnostic feature patterns were examined using random forest models and topographic stratification. The results show that village morphology is shaped by both basic SVSU-level types and their compositional relationships, producing compact, linear, dispersed, and mixed village-level types. Among the 33 multi-SVSU villages, 22 showed scale mismatch between conventional and multi-scale identification. Morphology diversity emerged as a structural correlate of scale mismatch, while SVSU number, dominant SVSU proportion, and topographic type were not significant. SDE and MBR showed higher diagnostic importance than building agglomeration indicators in differentiating assigned SVSU types. Topographic context modified the relative diagnostic importance of morphology indicators. The framework provides spatial evidence for identifying internally heterogeneous traditional villages and supports more differentiated conservation planning.
keywords: Conservation planning; Internal morphological diversity; Multi-scale spatial analysis; Scale mismatch; Sub-village spatial units; Traditional villages

abstract: The rapid expansion of the digital economy has generated substantial environmental costs, necessitating a reconciliation between digital growth and ecological sustainability. Green finance has emerged as a policy instrument to address this tension, yet empirical evidence remains limited. This study investigates whether and how China’s green finance pilot policy drives the green transformation of the digital economy (GTDE). Using panel data from 288 prefecture-level cities (2012–2022) and a framework integrating dynamic DML, spatial quantile DML, and causal forest simulation, we find that the policy significantly promotes GTDE, with an effect of 0.0079–0.0082 (a 6–7% improvement). Dynamic effects peak four years post-implementation. Three mechanisms operate: green credit support (22.4%), clean energy adoption in the digital industry (16.2%), and green technology diffusion (15.8%). Spatial analysis reveals a siphon effect within 150 km, positive spillovers between 150 and 200 km, and decay beyond 200 km. Heterogeneity shows stronger effects in cities with high financial development, stringent environmental regulations, and high human capital. Counterfactual simulations predict a 6.0% GTDE gain if the policy is expanded to all non-pilot cities. These findings offer causal evidence that green finance can drive the green transformation of the digital economy.
keywords: Causal forest; Dual machine learning; Green finance pilot policy; Green transformation of digital economy; Policy evaluation; Spatial quantile analysis

abstract: Built environments influence mental health, yet evidence on how different dimensions of urban form relate to specific mental health outcomes remains mixed, particularly in high-density cities. This study examined these relationships in Tehran, Iran, while accounting for spatial dependence and exploring spatial heterogeneity. Using secondary neighborhood-level data from 356 neighborhoods, five mental health outcomes—anxiety, depression, social dysfunction, somatic symptoms, and overall psychological distress—were analyzed in relation to the built environment. Ordinary Least Squares (OLS), Spatial Durbin Models (SDM), and Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR) were employed to assess global associations, spatial spillover effects, and localized spatial variation. The findings indicate that residential density emerged as the built-environment characteristic most consistently associated with poorer mental health, whereas population density showed no significant direct association with any mental health outcome. Access to daily services were associated with lower somatic symptoms and social dysfunction. Anxiety and depression were explained mainly by neighborhood socio-demographic characteristics, particularly unemployment and neighborhood age structure. Spatial spillover effects were identified only for social dysfunction, while exploratory GWR analyses indicated that neighborhood–mental health associations were predominantly global across Tehran, with only modest evidence of localized spatial variation. These findings demonstrate that different dimensions of urban density have distinct implications for mental health and that different mental health outcomes respond to different neighborhood characteristics. Overall, the results suggest that improving the quality of high-density residential environments, alongside addressing neighborhood socioeconomic inequalities, may be more effective than focusing on urban density alone when promoting mental health in high-density cities.
keywords: Accessibility; Mental health; Mix land use; Residential density; Spatial analysis

abstract: Rapid globalization and urbanization have triggered profound transformations in Rural Production Space System (RPSS), driving its functional orientation from production dominance to consumption dominance. Exploring this transformation process and analyzing its complex driving mechanisms can provide theoretical references for understanding rural transformation in the mountainous and hilly areas of southwestern China as well as in similar regions worldwide, and are of great significance for achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). This study develops a theoretical analytical framework for RPSS transformation from production to consumption. Taking Chongqing as the study area, and based on the evaluation of production and consumption levels of RPSS, the Tapio decoupling model and the GPI model are employed to identify the transformation types of RPSS and to reveal driving mechanisms. The results show that: (1) The production and consumption levels of the RPSS in Chongqing exhibited a trend of coordinated growth, with high-value areas of the production level concentrated in the Western Chongqing Region, while high-value areas of the consumption level were mainly located in central urban areas; (2) From 2013 to 2022, RPSS transformation in Chongqing was dominated by the consumption-led growth type and exhibited distinct stage-based changes, with consumption-led growth type prevailing from 2013 to 2017, and the proportions of production-led growth type and balanced growth type increasing from 2017 to 2022; (3) County-level fiscal capacity is the core factor influencing the spatial differentiation of RPSS transformation, and the driving factors of different transformation types exhibit significant differences and interaction effects.
keywords: Driving mechanisms; Mountainous and hilly areas; Post-productivism; Rural production space system; Stage-specific transition pathways; Tapio decoupling model

abstract: Urban scaling identifies economic performance relative to the output expected from population size but does not, by itself, identify why particular places depart from that benchmark. We examine whether population mobility and network position are associated with scale-adjusted economic performance (SAEP) in China’s Pearl River Delta (PRD) during 2019–2023. Annual SAEP is the residual from the GDP–population scaling relationship. Spatial panel models relate SAEP to intercity and intracity flows, directional imbalance, and network centrality across weekdays, weekends, and holidays, with robustness and endogeneity checks. The population hierarchy remained broadly stable, with only slight flattening, while spatial differences in SAEP persisted. Some weekday and weekend flow coefficients were statistically significant in parsimonious models but weakened in full specifications and were not robust across sensitivity analyses. Network centrality added little explanatory information. The spatial autoregressive coefficient was consistently negative and significant, indicating conditional spatial contrast among neighboring units rather than causal displacement or siphoning. Reverse-direction and IV checks did not resolve causal ordering. These findings delimit the explanatory reach of aggregate mobility: flow and centrality are relational proxies and do not identify a general mechanism of SAEP variation.
keywords: Network centrality; Pearl River Delta (PRD); Population mobility; Scale-adjusted economic performance (SAEP); Urban scaling

abstract: With the continuous improvement of China’s high-speed transportation system and the deepening of regional integration, intercity travel has become increasingly frequent and has emerged as an important field for studying spatial linkages and regional interaction among cities. Based on AMap Migration big data, we analyze the monthly rhythms and seasonal fluctuations of intercity travel throughout 2023. By examining flow characteristics at the national, city, and city-pair scales, this study reveals the monthly rhythm of intercity travel in China. Using K-means clustering and the temporal Gini coefficient, the study investigates the spatiotemporal patterns of intercity travel. The results show that intercity travel in China exhibits clear seasonality at the national scale, with peaks concentrated mainly in January, August, and October, and troughs concentrated in February–March and November–December. At the city scale, urban rhythmic patterns can be classified into four types: highly balanced, weak-rhythm, moderate-rhythm, and strong-rhythm. Economically developed large cities generally exhibit higher travel volumes and weaker seasonal fluctuations, whereas cities in western and northeastern regions tend to have smaller intercity travel volumes and stronger seasonal variability. At the city-pair scale, intercity travel with weaker seasonality is concentrated mainly within metropolitan areas and within the same province. These different types of cities and city pairs display marked differences in spatial distribution and travel demand. This study provides valuable insight into the seasonal patterns and spatial variation of intercity travel in China and has important theoretical and practical implications for urban transportation planning and policymaking.
keywords: Big data; Gini coefficient; Intercity travel; Monthly rhythm

abstract: Amid escalating global economic uncertainty and the resurgence of trade protectionism in developed economies, exports have become increasingly important as a key driver of China’s economic growth, particularly under the deepening implementation of the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI). Existing studies have mainly focused on how economic structure, geographical location, and export complexity affect export resilience, while the role of bilateral political relations in shaping national trade patterns has received relatively limited attention. To address this gap, this study constructs political proximity using Chinese Customs trade data and CEPII bilateral political relations data covering the period from 2003 to 2019. It further quantifies the impact of political proximity on China’s export resilience and conducts heterogeneity analyses across provinces and products. The results show that: (1) during the early period (2003–2012), political proximity had no significant effect on provincial export resilience but exerted a significantly negative effect on product-level export resilience; (2) during the later period (2013–2019), following the launch of the Belt and Road Initiative, political proximity significantly enhanced export resilience at both the provincial and product levels; (3) the impact of political proximity on the export resilience of provinces with different levels of technology and products varies significantly. By incorporating political factors into the analytical framework of China’s export resilience, this study provides new evidence on the role of political linkages in shaping international trade and offers valuable policy implications for developing countries seeking to strengthen export resilience under an increasingly complex and uncertain global trading environment.
keywords: China; Evolutionary economic geography; Export resilience; High-tech products; Political proximity

abstract: Rural settlements form a fundamental layer of cultural heritage, yet most existing studies analyse their distribution at a single temporal cross-section, leaving the dynamics of historical restructuring underexplored. This study constructs a multi-temporal GIS framework to reconstruct rural settlement distributions in the North China Plain at three time slices (1630, 1644, and 1680) spanning the Ming to Qing dynastic transition. Using 13,961 contemporary village locations as a spatial baseline, historical presence is estimated through toponymic analysis, administrative record linkage, and a probabilistic attrition model. Spatial pattern methods, Geodetector, and multiscale geographically weighted regression are then applied to trace disruption and recovery and to identify the geographic factors associated with settlement survival. Results indicate that the settlement total declined by a net 18.1% between 1630 and 1644, with only partial recovery by 1680 leaving the total 12.5% below the late Ming baseline. Loss was spatially concentrated in the western uplands of Zhangde Fu and the southern margins of Weihui Fu. Overlap analysis with the national traditional village inventory identifies over 7,400 model-classified persistent settlements that are not currently included in the heritage protection framework and may warrant further field verification. The findings provide a replicable template for event-scale settlement research and empirical grounding for heritage inventory refinement.
keywords: Heritage inventory; Ming–Qing transition; Multi-temporal GIS; North China Plain; Rural settlement; Spatial restructuring

abstract: Enhancing public service delivery is vital for improving residents’ well-being and advancing high-quality urban development. China’s push for urban digital-intelligent transformation provides new opportunities to strengthen the efficiency, quality, and accessibility of public services. We measure public service delivery levels across cities and uses the establishment of National AI Innovation Pilot Zones as a quasi-natural experiment. Employing a multi-period difference-in-differences framework, it examines the causal impact of digital-intelligent transformation on public service delivery and investigates its underlying mechanisms. The results show that urban digital-intelligent transformation significantly improves public service delivery. Mechanism tests indicate that the improvements operate mainly through enhanced urban innovation capacity and industrial upgrading. Heterogeneity analysis reveals stronger effects in southern regions, economically developed cities, and higher-level administrative units. Spatial spillover analysis further shows that NAIIPZs not only benefit pilot cities but also generate positive externalities for surrounding areas. However, the moderating analysis suggests that high fiscal decentralization weakens the positive impact of digital-intelligent transformation. This study enriches the literature on urban public services and offers policy insights for China’s urban modernization and global urban governance.
keywords: Fiscal decentralization; Multi-period difference-in-differences approach; Public service delivery; Urban digital-intelligent transformation

abstract: This study verified the effects of “experiential practice” and “visualizing” carbon dioxide reduction on the transformation of junior high school students' environmental awareness and pro-environmental behavior (PEB). We sought to propose measures for sustaining high environmental awareness and choice of appropriate actions. Based on a specific case study from the “Toride City Sustainable Learning Project” in Toride City, Ibaraki Prefecture, the following 2 hypotheses were tested: (1) combining knowledge acquisition with experiential practice effectively sustains PEB, and (2) enhancing responsibility yields the greatest outcomes. A comparative analysis was conducted between School B (knowledge-focused classes) and School A (4 -week decarbonization training program with carbon dioxide [CO₂] calculations). Results showed that School A had action implementation rates that were 2.0–3.4 times higher than those of School B for electricity conservation, water conservation and food waste reduction. Regression analysis revealed that “awareness of responsibility” was a statistically significant factor in sustaining PEB. Text mining indicated that School A students linked daily actions to quantifiable CO₂ reductions, enabling them to perceive global challenges as “personal issues” and recognize their roles. These findings suggest that behavioral change in lower secondary students occurs when they move beyond knowledge acquisition by gaining fresh insights through “visualizing decarbonization” and developing a sense of ownership and responsibility. We propose environmental education programs that guide students from “knowledge” to “behavioral reinforcement” through continuous experiential practice, thereby fostering ownership and responsibility.
keywords: Awareness of responsibility; Behavioral transformation; Education for sustainable development (ESD); Pro-environmental behavior (PEB); Secondary education; Visualization of CO₂ reduction

abstract: Household consumption accounts for approximately 60 percent of Brazil's GDP. Accurate representation of this component in applied economic models requires accounting for household preferences to capture spending heterogeneity across income groups. This paper is the first to estimate parameters of a Stone-Geary utility function for Brazil, covering 31 productive sectors and ten household income deciles. Results reveal a negative relationship between income and subsistence spending share in total expenditure, especially for food and housing. Higher-income households allocate a greater proportion of their income to services, such as private education, healthcare, tourism, culture, and recreation. The estimated parameters are applied in Computable General Equilibrium (CGE) simulations to evaluate their importance. Compared to a non-parameterized scenario, the estimated model yields 30% smaller GDP impacts, 40% smaller sectoral output effects, and heterogeneous shifts in consumption patterns, including 15 times higher impacts on imports and 6 times greater impacts on insurance by top-income households.
keywords: computable general equilibrium; Consumer behavior; demand elasticity; linear expenditure system

abstract: This paper contributes to the literature on demand estimation from survey data and the integration of consumer demand with macro-models. We estimate and analyze EU-wide and country-specific results of (modified) Taylor's [The Internal Structure of U.S. Consumption Expenditures. Springer.] intra-budget regressions, providing insights into the internal structure and interdependencies of European households' consumption expenditures. We propose a modified Taylor consumer demand system by properly incorporating the household budget constraint into the Taylor micro-model and derive closed-form expressions for price and income elasticities. We then integrate the modified Taylor micro-model with an open input-output (IO) quantity setting, analyzing both the non-linear and linearized IO micro-macro systems. The linearized framework enables the integration of any demand system into an IO model, supporting the analysis of consumer price impacts. Finally, we introduce and empirically examine novel multiplier matrices that capture the impacts of price changes on consumption, income, and production, and analyze the effects of consumer price increases in the EU.
keywords: distributional analysis; Household expenditure model; intra-budget coefficients; micro-macro modeling; micro-macro twins

abstract: This paper presents important model features for covering the socioeconomic impacts and the energy system dynamics of energy transition. For that, the standard IO model is extended to an energy system-IO model by linking to partial bottom-up energy models. The treatment of energy demand deviates from standard energy/environment CGE models by including energy (E) as a capital-stock specific demand. The IO core of the model identifies energy and non-energy industry linkages. Investments can shift the output shares across different energy-related technologies (e.g. from blast-furnace to electric-arc steel). This mechanism is consistently linked to the IO structure by applying a two-layered framework, i.e. energy flows are measured in both monetary and physical units. The impacts of energy transition on income distribution across households can be modelled by introducing ten different household/labour types.
keywords: energy input-output model; Energy transition; macroeconomic input-output model

abstract: This paper presents a matrix balancing technique based on Generalized Cross-Entropy (GCE) that can be suitable for matrices containing both positive and negative entries. One comparative advantage of the technique presented here is that it allows for the incorporation of inference into the estimates. An additional advantage is that this technique makes possible sign flips in the cells of the initial and the estimated matrices, which can be something desirable in situations where assuming sign-preservation for all the entries of the matrix could be too restrictive. A simple illustrative example shows how GCE works when adjusting a matrix characterized by having positive and negative entries within a Supply and Use Tables (SUT) framework, producing comparatively better indicators of error than other adjusting techniques.
keywords: generalized cross entropy; Matrix updating; sign preservation; statistical inference; supply and use tables

abstract: Despite its relevance for global mitigation, quantifying scope-3 emissions at the city level remains challenging. This study presents a consumption-based carbon footprint of Madrid over 2010–2023, integrating municipal data, regional supply and use tables, the FIGARO multiregional input–output database, and the first air emissions account for the city. The household CF fell from 31,135 (Formula presented.) in 2010 to 21,308 (Formula presented.) in 2023, with per capita emissions at 6113 (Formula presented.) and over 55% of emissions coming from international supply chains. Distributional analysis reveals pronounced carbon inequality: high-expenditure households emitted 5.2 times more than the lowest-expenditure quintile. Simulations suggest that reshaping expenditure patterns among top-spending households and fostering limited carbon-neutral transport adoption could jointly reduce the household CF by 29.6%. These findings underscore the need for consumption-focused mitigation strategies to complement Madrid’s Roadmap toward Climate Neutrality.
keywords: Carbon footprint; cities; input–output; mitigation

abstract: This paper analyses the potential effect of automation on the global portfolio of trade specialization and income distribution based on the principle of comparative advantage, employed in an extension of Duchin's World Trade Model to include non-tradable sectors. Through a futuristic scenario-based analysis within the global economic context and using data from the World Input–Output Database and the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC), we find that developing countries, particularly in lower-income Asia (including China, India, and Indonesia) are likely to be the most adversely affected by reshoring induced by automation adoption, whereas advanced economies benefit at their expense. The manufacturing sector in the developing countries is the most vulnerable to automation-driven reshoring.
keywords: AI; automation; global trade model; Input–output model; reshoring

abstract: Disasters often disrupt supply chains, leading to cascading effects across regions. Regions not directly hit by the disaster may attempt to compensate for the lost production, but their ability to do so is constrained by their available production capacity and the logistical constraints between regions. This study introduces a Multi-Regional Impact Assessment (MRIA) model to evaluate the economic impact of disasters, capturing post-disaster trade dynamics and logistical constraints. The model uses EU interregional Supply and Use tables from Eurostat and is implemented for case studies in the Netherlands. Our findings emphasize that enhancing production capacity alone is inadequate; regional trade flexibility must also be improved to mitigate impacts. At the regional level, disaster-affected areas experience severe negative impacts, whereas larger, export-oriented regions benefit from increased production activity. Additionally, we propose a sectoral criticality assessment that effectively identifies sectors with low redundancy while accounting for regional substitution in a post-disaster scenario.
keywords: criticality analysis; Disasters; input–output; macroeconomic impacts; multi-regional

abstract: This paper contributes to the literature on cross-border impacts at the global level of compound, climate-related multi-hazards. Our study examines the economic damage to Europe from alternative realizations (along storylines) of cyclones in the United States, China, and Japan by coupling natural hazard risk models that estimate the immediate, direct physical costs of hazards with a global recursive dynamic computable general equilibrium model. This approach offers two innovations. First, we assess cross-border impacts of compound natural hazards at the global level and across sectors using a computable general equilibrium model. This goes beyond the conventional narrow focus on a single sector, region, or hazard. Second, we assess the financial sector's role as a transmission channel for cross-border impacts. The results demonstrate material impacts for Europe. While the financial sector can absorb shocks in the short run, the resulting investment decisions reorient international financial flows, creating negative, long-lasting effects worldwide.
keywords: Climate change; compound multi-hazard risk; cross-border economic impacts; cross-border financial impacts; extreme events

abstract: In the context of global climate change, one of the biggest challenges is water security. In Brazil, long-term climate anomalies and regional water resource disparities may constrain various socioeconomic activities. We developed an integrated assessment model (IAM) for the Brazilian hydrographic regions. The economic losses resulting from the effect of climate change on water availability are equivalent to a drop in Brazilian GDP (year reference 2015) of US$ 5.2 billion [US$ 3.2B to US$ 7.7B] and US$ 12.5 billion [US$ 7.8B to US$ 18.6B] under RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5 (by 2070–2099). Highlights Integrated assessment models are robust tools to assess the water-economy impacts. Brazilian GDP may drop US$ 12.5 billion due to changes in water availability. Economic sectors and regions respond differently to water availability shocks. Climate change may significantly impact the water and sewage sector, with negative effects under water scarcity and positive effects where water availability increases.
keywords: Brazilian hydrographic regions; climate change; computable general equilibrium model; integrated assessment model; water

abstract: Equitable access to higher education remains a pressing challenge, particularly for underrepresented and marginalized groups. Financial aid is one of the most important policy tools for addressing these disparities, yet allocation decisions are often guided by ad hoc rules that neither systematically enforce fairness nor optimize the use of limited institutional resources. This can undermine both the effectiveness and the equity of financial aid policies. In this paper, we study financial aid allocation as a fairness-aware resource allocation problem for continuing higher education students. We formulate the problem as an Integer Programming (IP) model that maximizes aggregate predicted student success subject to unique-allocation, limited-budget, Per-Capita Fairness (PCF), and Equal Opportunity Fairness (EOF) constraints. Student success probabilities are estimated from historical data using a Random Forest classifier. Because solving the exact IP formulation can be computationally expensive, we develop an LP relaxation coupled with a randomized rounding based on permutation selection . The proposed rounding framework first expands the LP solution into a column-stochastic matrix and then pads it to obtain a doubly stochastic matrix. It subsequently applies the Birkhoff algorithm to sample a permutation-based integer allocation. We provide theoretical analysis for the proposed LP-relaxation approach. In particular, we prove that the permutation-selection-based rounding is unbiased with respect to the expanded LP solution, show that the padded matrix used by the rounding procedure is doubly stochastic, prove that the EO and PC fairness constraints are satisfied in expectation after rounding, and characterize the overall computational complexity of the LP-relaxation framework. We evaluate the framework on a real educational dataset under two budget scenarios and multiple fairness-aware optimization settings. The results show that the LP-based approach achieves near-optimal objective values relative to the IP model while substantially reducing computational burden. The experiments also demonstrate that activating fairness constraints markedly improves fairness scores across demographic groups, with only a limited reduction in the objective value. These findings highlight the practical potential of fairness-aware predictive and prescriptive analytics for designing transparent, resource-efficient, and equity-conscious financial aid policies.
keywords: Fairness; Financial aid allocation; Integer programming; LP relaxation; Randomized rounding; Resource allocation

abstract: In this paper, we calculate the two-sided (consumer and producer) market accessibility of the Greek islands, based on different measures of transport cost, namely, the actual network distance and the freight shipment cost from/to mainland regions and between them. For this purpose, we employ a unique micro-dataset of 1,026,469 shipments for the year 2021 originated from the platform of Islands’ Transport Equivalent for firms. The shipment cost refers to the receipts of payments made by firms for outsourcing transport services to companies with public-use truck vehicles. The findings show the importance of the population size, geographical proximity to large markets and network connectivity, and underscore the severe imbalances among consumers’ (importers’) and producers’ (exporters’) accessibility to and from the Greek islands. Moreover, the use of shipment cost significantly alters the accessibility hierarchy and trade imbalance inequalities among islands, as it incorporates insularity theory-consistent and inherent characteristics of the logistics and product markets. Relevant policy implications are made to support the design of more effective island policies aimed at supporting the competitiveness of local businesses, the living standards of inhabitants and the territorial cohesion of the country.
keywords: Accessibility; Freight transport; Greece; Island Transport Equivalent; Network distance; Shipment cost

abstract: Rural development in Sub-Saharan Africa is mostly measured by economic indicators, despite growing calls to broaden this narrow focus. Although wellbeing is used in discourse, it often repackages economic goals rather than capturing people’s subjective wellbeing. We address this gap by analysing how and why agricultural intensification, commercialisation and infrastructure interventions affect life satisfaction, a central component of subjective wellbeing, among Tanzanian smallholder farmers within the Southern Agricultural Growth Corridor of Tanzania (SAGCOT). Using longitudinal survey data from 2019 and 2023 (N = 871) and focus groups, we show that life satisfaction has increased on average. Among the variables analysed in this study, access to electricity combined with Information and Communication Technologies (ICT) use is associated with higher life satisfaction. Despite development narratives, we do not find statistically significant evidence that agricultural intensification is associated with higher life satisfaction. Commercialisation is negatively associated with life satisfaction, which our qualitative findings link to perceived structural and market barriers. Infrastructure effects are heterogeneous and depend on household access: road improvements are associated with lower satisfaction among households without transport, while electricity is associated with higher satisfaction when used for ICT. These findings show that life satisfaction provides a valuable lens for understanding the intended and unintended impacts of development and can inform policies and practices by highlighting that these impacts are heterogeneous and vary across different groups.
keywords: Agricultural development; Infrastructure development; Life satisfaction; Rural wellbeing; Tanzania

abstract: Expanding renewable energy in developing countries is essential for achieving global sustainable development and fighting climate change. However, many developing economies face financial constraints that limit their capacity to invest in renewable energy technologies despite increasing international climate commitments. This study examines the role of international public financial support in promoting renewable energy use across thirty-six developing countries from 2000 to 2020. It employs panel cointegration techniques and the pooled mean-group autoregressive distributed lag model to explore long-term relationships among renewable energy consumption, international public financial flows, income levels, per capita carbon emissions, and government effectiveness. Additionally, it uses quantile regression and panel causality analyses to ensure robustness. The quantile findings indicate that public investment flows have a positive and significant effect on renewable consumption at low-to-moderate quantiles, but become insignificant at higher quantiles, likely because external public finance is more effective in supporting countries at earlier stages of renewable energy adoption than those with more mature renewable energy systems. Income levels also positively influence renewable energy adoption, while government effectiveness shows no significant impact. The causality analysis indicates a bidirectional relationship between international financial support and renewable energy use, with income exerting a unidirectional influence on renewable energy consumption. The findings highlight the importance of strengthening international cooperation, improving the allocation of climate finance, and supporting strategic investments in sustainable energy infrastructure to achieve SDGs 7 and 13 in developing nations.
keywords: Developing economies; Institutional quality; International financial flows; Public investments; Renewable energy consumption

abstract: This paper derives incentives for voluntary interregional coordination and the conditions for coordination agreements using a model of non-cooperative provision of regional public goods targeting multiple regions. The interregional coordination discussed here is limited to two areas. The first is a policy to coordinate the relaxation of restrictions on access to regional public goods by residents of other regions. The second is to relax access to public goods in one region for residents of other regions and, in return, receive transfers from other regions. Under such circumstances, the incentive for regions to coordinate with each other is that regional coordination will improve the welfare of each region beyond its initial state. This requires that the coordination policy be Pareto-improving. If this transfer is partial, it corresponds to the partial outsourcing of public goods provision to other regions. If all public goods are outsourced to other regions and all public funds are transferred in return, this corresponds to a situation of merger (absorption), in which the region is completely absorbed by other regions. The former consists of the transfer of financial resources for the provision of joint public goods, while the latter consists of the complete outsourcing of public goods provision. To analyze these issues, we first present a public goods game for two regions and examine the regional coordination problem. I then show that the coordinated relaxing of public goods access is Pareto-improving. Furthermore, we derive the conditions under which regional coordination can be achieved when interregional transfers are available. Next, I apply the analysis of the two region model to the coordination problem between the central city and several neighboring regions. This central city-neighboring regions model reflects the actual structure of interregional coordination, and therefore identifies the conditions for agreement on regional coordination. From the analysis of regional coordination, when the initial state is non-cooperative, it can be shown that 1) if all regions are completely identical, cooperative relaxation of access to public goods improves the welfare of each region; 2) if regions are asymmetric, the degree of relaxation of access also differs between regions; and 3) if interregional transfers are available as compensation for unilateral relaxation of access to public goods, such regional coordination is Pareto-improving.
keywords: Intergovernmental transfer; Interregional coordination; Local public goods; Transfer paradox

abstract: In this paper, we used the D9SCGE model to clarify the impact of two agricultural policies, namely the promotion of the active utilization of smart agricultural technology and the promotion of exports of agricultural, forestry and fishery products and food, on Japan’s food self-sufficiency ratio and regional economy through the expansion of domestic agricultural and food production. The following points were clarified in this paper. First, a cost-benefit analysis of the policy goals stipulated in the Act on Promot ing the Utilization of Smart Agricultual Technology showed that if smart agricultural technology was used on most cultivated areas by 2035 with the current budget scale and the government’s target of agricul tural labor productivity of 5% or more was achieved, the benefits （equivalent variance） did not exceed the total costs （cumulative budget amount）. In order for the benefits to exceed the total costs, it is nec essary to consider a policy framework for raising agricultural labor productivity to 6-7%. Second, if the productivity of the agricultural sector increased to the same level as the potential growth rate and land intensification was promoted, Japan’s food self-sufficiency rate did not exceed the 2025 level estimated from this model unless two agricultural policies, the spread of smart agricultural technology and export expansion measures, were implemented. For this reason, if these two agricultural policies were steadily implemented, Japan’s food self-sufficiency rate increased by 2% to 3% from the 2025 level by 2050. Third, with regard to the impact on the regional economy, if productivity in each industry increased to the level of potential growth, the GRP in the Tohoku region was heavily affected by the population decline, and grew only 0.3% by 2035, and was almost zero by 2050. On the other hand, it was found that the GRP in the Kanto and Chubu regions grew at a rate higher than the potential growth rate. Thus, look ing at the impact on agricultural production in a situation where the gap in the regional economies between urban and rural areas was expected to widen due to the population decline, it was found that with the spread of smart agricultural technology and measures to expand exports, agricultural production in Tohoku, Kinki, and Shikoku grew 0.1% to 0.3% between 2035 and 2050, and Hokkaido, Kanto, and Kyushu, with a high weighting of agricultural production, was able to secure a growth rate of 0.6% to 0.7%.
keywords: Agricultural Productivity; Dynamic Interregional CGE Model; Food Export; Self–sufficiency Ratio; Smart Agriculture

abstract: This study aimed to evaluate the effects of different cover materials on environmental efficiency in controlled environment horticulture, taking into consideration the regional characteristics of Wakayama Prefecture. First, model facilities and cultivation conditions for controlled environment horticulture were established at multiple cultivation sites within Wakayama Prefecture. Subsequently, existing cover materials widely used in the field were selected, and comparisons constructed by combining these materials. Next, tools such as yield estimation, improved fuel estimation, and equipment introduction estimation tools were used to calculate greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and business revenues. Finally, environmental efficiency was calculated based on the derived GHG emissions and business revenues. The results showed that Ethylene Tetrafluoroethylene (ETFE) agricultural film had the highest environmental efficiency in all evaluation regions, while Polyolefin (PO) agricultural film had the lowest environmental efficiency. Furthermore, there were significant differences in environmental efficiency between regions, with the largest variation observed in Pattern 3 (PT3) (outer layer : ethylene tetrafluoroethylene film – inner layer : agricultural vinyl film) and the smallest in Pattern 2 (PT2) (outer layer : agricultural polyolefin film – inner layer : agricultural polyolefin film). The differences in environmental efficiency between regions were strongly influenced by fluctuations in heating loads due to the use of heating oil, reaffirming that the environmental efficiency of agricultural cover materials are significantly affected by regional climate conditions. These results confirm that achieving decarbonization and sustainability in facility horticulture requires evaluations tailored to regional conditions. The combination of cover materials in PT3 demonstrated relatively low greenhouse gas emissions and the potential to increase sales revenue, suggesting the importance of selecting optimal cover materials based on regional climate characteristics. To improve environmental efficiency in the future, it is necessary to consider not only the selection of cover materials but also the introduction of low-carbon heating technologies such as heat pumps and combinations of carbon dioxide dispersion methods tailored to regional conditions. A strategic approach that takes regional characteristics into account is essential, rather than a one-size-fits-all approach. Future challenges include optimizing planting times by region and analyzing the aging degradation of inner cover materials.
keywords: CO2 enrichment; cover materials; eco-efficiency; greenhouse horticulture; Wakayama Prefecture

abstract: The purpose of this study was to clarify recent changes in the rice purchasing behavior of Japanese consumers through an analysis of the e-commerce (EC) market, with particular attention on the transformation of market structure and shift in brand perception from an information-based to a meaning-based orientation. Two hypotheses were established: (1) Japan's rice EC market functions as a monopolistic competition market characterized by product differentiation; and (2) consumer brand perception is shifting from information-based brand value — derived from objective product attributes — to meaning-based brand value co-created through consumption experience and reviews. To verify these hypotheses, product data were collected from three types of EC platforms — specialized rice stores, direct-from-producer sites and general e-commerce sites — and were analyzed using a hedonic pricing model. The results showed that attributes such as brand (variety × production area), certification and small package size have statistically significant effects on prices across all platforms. These findings support Hypothesis 1 and indicate that the rice EC market indeed functions as a differentiated monopolistic competition market. Moreover, platform-specific patterns were observed: specialized stores show relatively concentrated price ranges for well-known brands, direct-from-producer sites show wide price dispersion reflecting strong consumer commitment to specific producers and regional identities, and general EC platforms show clear associations between rating patterns and price formation, suggesting an active role of reviews in shaping perceived value. Taken together, these results support Hypothesis 2, demonstrating that brand meaning in the rice EC market is increasingly constructed through consumer experiences and post-purchase evaluations. Based on these findings, three strategic implications for the rice industry can be identified. First, flexible branding strategies tailored to channel-specific consumer characteristics are essential — for example, emphasizing reliability and consistency in specialty channels, while highlighting producer narratives and regional identity in channels where individuality is valued. Second, consumer reviews should be regarded not merely as "word-of-mouth" but as mechanisms for co-creating brand meaning. Therefore, encouraging detailed reviews and integrating Social Networking Service platforms can enhance active consumer participation in value formation. Third, increasing transparency regarding certifications and production processes, expanding 1-2 kg package offerings, and optimizing total payment structures — including both item price and shipping costs — can simultaneously appeal to consumer demands for safety, freshness and convenience. Overall, in an EC environment characterized by diverse purchasing channels and active redefinition of brand meaning by consumers, adopting flexible and strategic value propositions aligned with channel characteristics are crucial for securing competitive advantage in Japan's rice market.
keywords: Consumer behavior; EC market; Hedonic pricing approach; Japan; Rice

abstract: Following the relaxation of COVID-19 travel restrictions, the number of inbound tourists has rapidly recovered, surpassing 2019 levels. However, this recovery has led to the concentration of tourists in specific urban areas, causing over-tourism issues, while many rural regions still struggle to attract sufficient visitors. To address this regional disparity and promote sustainable tourism, it is crucial to quantitatively understand the determinants of where tourists choose to stay. This study empirically analyzed the factors influencing the staying population of inbound tourists across 1,896 municipalities in Japan, utilizing location-based big data (KDDI Location Analyzer) from the entire year of 2023. Multiple regression analysis was employed to examine the impact of socio-economic factors — such as population density, the number of accommodation employees and proximity to transport hubs — and various tourism resources, including World Heritage sites, National Treasures, hot spring resorts (onsen) and castles. The analysis classified the data by visit frequency (first-time vs. repeaters), time of day, visitor origin (Asia vs. Europe), and region (Golden Route vs. Rural areas) to capture diverse tourist needs. The results of the comprehensive analysis were as follows. First, regarding the total staying population, basic infrastructure (population density and accommodation capacity) and proximity to international airports significantly increased the number of stays. Among tourism resources, hot spring resorts (onsen) demonstrated a consistently strong positive influence. Second, regarding visit frequency, repeat visitors exhibited a much higher affinity for stay-oriented resources like onsen compared to first-time visitors, who were more sensitive to transport accessibility. Third, the analysis by time of day revealed a behavioral cycle where tourists visit attraction sites during the day and congregate in accommodation-dense areas at night. Fourth, a distinct contrast was observed based on visitor origin: Asian tourists prioritized transport efficiency and airport access, whereas European tourists showed a marked preference for historical and cultural assets, such as World Heritage sites and castles. Finally, the regional comparison indicates that while the Golden Route relies heavily on transportation convenience and historical-cultural assets, rural areas depend more on natural resources and stay-type tourism resources to attract visitors. In addition, this study demonstrates that a combination of location-based big data and statistical models is an effective method for quantitatively verifying regional differences in the inbound staying population and their association with regional characteristics. The results of this analysis provide useful basic information for formulating promotion initiatives, future tourism policy planning, and regional revitalization strategies.
keywords: Inbound Staying Population; Location-Based Big Data; Multiple Regression Analysis; Tourism Resources

abstract: Multi-country input-output tables quantitatively represent transaction flows across industries and countries and provide an important empirical basis for studying global value chains (GVCs) and regional economics. In recent years, a trend toward “big government” has been observed in advanced economies such as the United States, where industrial policies are actively promoted. Meanwhile, international trade relations have developed beyond bilateral transactions into multilateral, interdependent networks, and the importance of GVC studies using multi-country input-output tables is accordingly increasing. To this end, we propose a new extended method that constructs minimum spanning trees (MSTs) representing transaction structures using Z-scores, visualizes them by incorporating GVC lengths and industry categories, and quantitatively evaluates the significance of nodes in terms of centrality measures. In this paper, we call this method the pair-type MST method. In the experimental evaluation of the proposed pair-type MST method, we conducted both qualitative and quantitative analyses using the World Input-Output Tables (WIOTs) available from the World Input-Output Database (WIOD) and the Inter-Country Input-Output (ICIO) tables provided by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). In the quantitative analysis, we introduce new indicators such as GVC length, input coefficient centrality, and output coefficient centrality, and compared the industry-based MST with the country-based MST to examine structural differences. The results confirm that the industry-node backbone structure is robust and stable. As an implication for regional economic research, although trade relations among certain countries have changed significantly over the past two decades due to institutional transitions and other factors, the backbone structure among industries has remained stable, partly because of shifts in the roles of countries within the global trade network.
keywords: Global Value Chains; Industry-Node Backbone Structures; Multi-Country Input-Output Tables; Pair-Type Minimum Spanning Tree Method; Visualization

abstract: This study applied the hypothetical extraction method （HEM） to the 2015 Chubu Region multi regional input-output table （comprising 45 sectors） to examine interregional linkages connecting Ishikawa Prefecture’s core industries : production machinery, textile products, electronic components and accommodations, with the Chubu Region. Simulated removal of each sector revealed interregional trade flows and quantified economic dependencies between Ishikawa and other prefectures within the Chubu Region. Manufacturing sectors （production machinery, textile products, and electronic compo nents） exhibited strong interregional linkages with both neighboring prefectures in the Hokuriku area and more distant prefectures in the Tokai area. By contrast and reflecting its reliance on region-specific services and cultural assets, the accommodation sector demonstrated a more localized impact. We iden tified two distinct patterns of industrial impact : i） affected sectors were consistent across regions, and ii） impacts varied according to regional trade structures. Ishikawa accounted for approximately 60% of the total production loss in each manufacturing sector, while the accommodation sector accounted for approximately 75%, thus indicating stronger local dependence. Furthermore, the affected industries in other prefectures included both highly and less specialized sectors, with varying degrees of impact. Considering the potential economic damage from large-scale disasters, the importance of incorporating interregional trade structures into disaster preparedness is underscored. Moreover, extending the HEM analysis to other Chubu Prefectures can enhance understanding of cross-regional vulnerabilities. This framework supports proactive planning for disaster mitigation, industrial development, and regional collaboration, ultimately contributing to more resilient and interconnected regional economies.
keywords: Chubu Region; Hypothetical Extraction Method; Multi-Regional Input-Output Table; Regional Linkage

abstract: This study aims to examine the influence of seven key factors on population movement from coastal to inland regions in China : disposable income, unemployment rate, housing prices, and local government expenditures on education, healthcare, social security and other public services. Using population movement data from the National Bureau of Statistics of China (2011; 2021), we apply a gravity model by comparing changes in these factors from 2010 to 2020. The results are as follows. First, regarding disposable income, no statistically significant effect on population migration was found in either coastal or inland regions in most models. However, the coefficient for inland areas shifted from negative to positive, suggesting that rising income is gradually beginning to promote population inflow into inland regions. Second, while an increase in the unemployment rate in coastal areas did not necessarily accelerate migration to inland areas, a rising unemployment rate in inland regions reduced utility and became a clear factor inhibiting population inflow in 2020. Third, rising housing prices in inland areas were found to promote population inflow; however, this effect showed a slight weakening by 2020. Fourth, in 2010, fiscal expenditures on education, healthcare, and social security in coastal areas helped suppress population outflow. In 2020, educational expenditures in inland areas became a significant factor in promoting population inflow. In contrast, the effects of healthcare and social security expenditures remained limited, suggesting that disparities in medical services and social security systems between regions persist. By focusing on the changes between 2010 and 2020, the analysis more clearly demonstrates the positive impact of expanded fiscal expenditures in inland areas as a significant driver of population inflows.
keywords: China; Fiscal expenditure; Gravity model; Population movement; Regional development

abstract: Edible insects have attracted attention as a potential source of sustainable food. However, as in other developed countries, Japanese consumers have exhibited low acceptance of insect-based foods. Existing studies on consumer preferences for edible insects have mainly focused on Europe and the United States, while evidence from Asia, Africa, and Latin America remains limited. In particular, few studies have examined consumer willingness to pay (WTP) for insect-based foods or assessed the effectiveness of acceptance-enhancing strategies in Japan. Improving consumer acceptance therefore requires an understanding of consumer preferences and WTP, as well as differentiation of insect-based foods from conventional products through attributes such as nutritional value. To address these gaps, this study conducted an online survey incorporating a discrete choice experiment targeting Japanese consumers. The analysis pursued two objectives : estimation of consumer WTP for snack products containing cricket powder and evaluation of the effect of nutritional information on WTP through random assignment to information and no-information groups. Choice data were analyzed using a mixed logit model to account for preference heterogeneity. The results showed that the marginal WTP for snack products containing cricket powder ranged from -108.5 to -76.6 yen relative to conventional snack products, indicating strong aversion to insect-based foods among Japanese consumers. In contrast, nutritional information had no statistically significant effect on WTP, suggesting that health- and nutrition-related information alone is insufficient to mitigate negative perceptions or emotional responses. This reflects a mismatch between the information provided and consumer needs, or the possibility that any positive informational effect is offset by the strongly negative baseline valuation of the product. Overall, the findings suggest that expanding acceptance of insect-based foods in Japan requires a multifaceted approach beyond nutritional attributes alone.
keywords: Choice Experiment; Consumer Preferences; Edible Insects; Mixed Logit Model; Nutritional Information Provision

abstract: This study examines the dynamics of regional income convergence in the European Union (EU) – specifically the EU27, now excluding the United Kingdom – to assess whether the Single Market continues to provide meaningful catch-up opportunities. The 2004–2021 period is particularly instructive for this question, as the major crises of the last two decades have had asymmetrical regional impacts. Building on the Mankiw–Romer–Weil framework, we estimate a conditional β-convergence model enriched with structural factors (investment, demographics, human capital, sectoral specialization and metropolitan status) and incorporate spatial dependence using a full set of spatial econometric models. The spatial Durbin model emerges as the most appropriate specification, capturing endogenous and exogenous interactions in a heterogeneous economic landscape. The results reveal that conditional convergence persists but remains slow and spatially uneven. Human capital deficits strongly hinder local and neighbouring regions’ growth, while knowledge-intensive services primarily generate internal benefits with limited spillover. Manufacturing is one of the few activities producing positive spatial effects, consistent with the role of European value-chain integration. Metropolitan regions enjoy internal advantages but do not systematically transmit growth to neighbouring regions, in a pattern partially shaped by administrative boundaries and spatial heterogeneity. Overall, the Single Market continues to support convergence, but only under specific structural and spatial conditions. Strengthening human capital, improving knowledge diffusion, deepening integration into value chains and reducing spatial fragmentation are essential to ensure more inclusive regional development across the EU.
keywords: conditional convergence; European Union; spatial econometrics; spatial effects

abstract: Slovak society after 1990 recorded unprecedented changes in almost all sectors. One of these changes is the transformation of religious relations, extensively measured mainly using population censuses, which still brings new challenges. This transformation sometimes appears to have different vectors at the societal level and others at the level of dynamic spaces significantly influenced by migration. Herein, we examine signs of change within the functional urban region of Bratislava, with particular attention to the city and its suburban areas, and especially to the transformation of age ratios. We hypothesized that as the suburban population grows, the fastest-expanding group would be those without religious affiliation. Migration to urban and suburban areas is not only a source of non-denominational population growth but also mitigates the ageing of main denominational groups and diversifies this space. Drawing on data from the 2001 and 2021 population censuses, we seek to capture these changes and illustrate the state of this dynamic through basic quantitative indicators. In a broader context, the analysis sheds light on the dynamics of processes such as suburban migration in a post-socialist city and their impact on the religious landscape of the region. This study thus offers an example of how suburbanization drives transformations not only in the physical environment but also in the cultural sphere.
keywords: Bratislava; functional urban region; migration; non-denominationalism; population ageing; religiosity

abstract: Life expectancy has increased substantially across Europe in recent decades, but improvements within countries have often been uneven across regions. Evidence on the long-term subnational experiences of post-communist countries remains limited. This study examines regional convergence in life expectancy at birth across Hungarian districts using σ- and β-convergence approaches from the 1980s to the early 2020s. σ-convergence is measured using the population-weighted standard deviation of life expectancy at birth. Changes in the standard deviation are decomposed into age-specific contributions of mortality (M) and population structure (P), separately for total, between-, and within-region components. District-level disparity (N = 175) increased over time: the standard deviation doubled among women and exceeded early-1990s crisis levels among men. Divergence was concentrated above age 50, particularly at ages 65 and over, whereas mortality below age 50 showed convergence. β-convergence models reveal regional polarization at older ages, reflecting faster improvements in the capital region and distinct convergence dynamics in the former heavy-industry region. These findings indicate that mortality convergence can only be understood by accounting for both age-specific dynamics and spatial heterogeneity.
keywords: age-specific dynamics; Hungary; life expectancy; mortality convergence; regional inequalities

abstract: A longstanding consensus in scientific discourse holds that the European population is ageing, with notable regional variation (Długosz 2011). Śídlo et al. (2019) analyse these differences at the regional level, concluding that the oldest populations are concentrated in Western and Southern Europe, while the youngest are found in Central and Eastern Europe. The present analysis seeks to illustrate the fundamental spatial pattern of the European age structure at the highest available resolution.
keywords: ageing; Europe; grid; spatial pattern

abstract: Evaluating the economic impact of trade policy in computable general equilibrium (CGE) models relies on the trade elasticities. This study builds a new, internally consistent database of trade elasticities that can be directly integrated into the CGE framework.We estimate a structural gravity model by Poisson pseudo maximum likelihood (PPML), using bilateral HS6 trade flows and applied tariff rates. The estimation yields elasticities for approximately 5,000 HS6 products, covering nearly the entire classification. The median elasticity is 5.28, and the 10th to 90th percentile span is 1.49 to 15.33, underscoring pronounced heterogeneity in price sensitivity.Each product is mapped to one of the 47 GTAP goods sectors, and the resulting elasticities are compared with the region-generic default values. The simulation experiments on U.S. tariff shocks are conducted using the estimated elasticities as well as the GTAP default parameters. The results reveal that the difference in elasticity affects bilateral imports of goods the most, leading to sign reversals of macroeconomic variables, including GDP, economic welfare, and real income for some countries.
keywords: CGE; Import tariffs; Trade elasticity

abstract: As economies become increasingly globalized and production processes are increasingly offshored, it has become essential to clarify the global supply chains to which each country’s industries belong. This study examines countries’ participation in global supply chains by analyzing how domestic industrial groups form networks that connect with global production systems. The approach of this paper consists of two steps. First, while Johnson and Noguera (2012) and Timmer et al. (2013) provided foundational frameworks for global value chain (GVC) analysis, this study introduces a new theoretical approach based on Ozaki’s (1980) unit structure analysis. Earlier studies estimate value added by defining destination countries as final consumers or producers, whereas Kuroiwa (2021) integrated unit structure analysis to present an alternative estimation of total value‑added flows to destination countries. Extending this framework, the present study identifies destination countries as importers involved in subsequent production stages and represents the upstream value‑added structure as a network. Second, using this framework and following Kagawa et al. (2015), this study employs network diagrams to analyze Japan’s automobile industry and its bilateral relationships with the U.S. and China from 2002 to 2022. The results highlight China’s development of domestic industrial networks that enable active participation in GVCs.
keywords: Global supply chain; Global value chain; Network analysis; Trade in value added; Unit structure analysis

abstract: This article assesses the impact of the digital economy on industry and the environment by comparing 15 countries (7 developed and 8 developing) over the period 2000–2021. Using the System Generalized Method of Moments (SYS-GMM), the analysis reveals contrasting results between country groups. For developed countries, a 1% increase in ICT imports is associated with a 0.159% reduction in CO₂ emissions (p-value < 0.01) and a marginal 0.038% decrease in industrial employment (p-value < 0.10), consistent with automation-driven labor reallocation toward high-value-added sectors. In developing countries, the same 1% increase in ICT imports yields an insignificant effect on CO₂ emissions (− 0.008, p-value = 0.676) and industrial employment (− 0.016, p-value = 0.113), reflecting structural constraints including outdated energy infrastructure and limited absorptive capacity for green technologies. Industrial value-added positively influences employment in both groups, though the elasticity is higher in developed economies (0.048 vs. 0.031). The results underscore the need for developed countries to sustain investments in advanced digital infrastructure and innovation policies that accelerate the green digital transition. For developing countries, priorities should include strengthening green digital infrastructure, fostering international technology-transfer partnerships, and implementing targeted workforce retraining programs to maximize the employment and environmental co-benefits of digitalization.
keywords: CO₂ emissions; Developed countries, Developing countries; Digital economy; Industrial employment; SYS-GMM

abstract: This study examines the convergence of healthcare expenditure and population health outcomes across eleven European countries from 2000 to 2019. Using the β-convergence framework and coefficient-of-variation analysis, the study investigates three health-expenditure indicators—health expenditure as a share of GDP, public health expenditure per capita, and private health expenditure per capita—and two health outcomes: life expectancy at birth and crude death rate. The full-sample results indicate evidence of convergence across several indicators. However, the regional analysis reveals substantial heterogeneity among Nordic, Baltic, and Central/Eastern European countries. The Nordic countries exhibit significant convergence in health expenditure as a share of GDP, public health expenditure per capita, and life expectancy. The Baltic countries show significant convergence across all three health-expenditure indicators but not in the health outcomes. Central/Eastern European countries exhibit significant convergence in private health expenditure and the two health outcomes, but not in health expenditure as a share of GDP or public health expenditure per capita. These findings demonstrate that convergence in healthcare expenditure does not necessarily translate into convergence in population health and that aggregate estimates may conceal important regional differences. The results suggest that healthcare expenditure alone may not ensure convergence in health outcomes, while institutional and structural mechanisms require further investigation through conditional convergence analysis.
keywords: Baltic countries; Central/Eastern Europe; Crude death rate; Health expenditure; Health outcomes; Life expectancy; Nordic countries; Regional heterogeneity; β-convergence

abstract: We examine the relationship between the implementation of the Basel III accord and the growth of non-bank financial institutions and fintech platforms in South Africa. Using difference-in-differences estimation procedures, we find evidence consistent with regulatory arbitrage. In particular, the imposition of minimum capital requirements is associated with stronger growth among constrained non-bank financial institutions relative to their unconstrained peers. Similarly, country-level estimations show that tighter minimum capital restrictions are associated with the growth of fintech platforms in South Africa, whereas innovation appears to be an important factor associated with the growth of fintech ventures in selected African economies. Our results highlight the need for targeted policies that enable and sustain a vibrant fintech ecosystem.
keywords: Basel III; COVID-19; fintech; innovation; non-bank financial institutions; venture capital funding

abstract: Team composition in sports rarely considers the significant mix of players in a national team's tournament performance. This study theorises that the mere inclusion of foreign-based nationals is not enough to guarantee team success, especially in the African Cup of Nations (AFCON) tournaments. Using panel data on AFCON records of participating national teams from 1990 to 2025 in an ordinal logit regression, we reveal that an over-reliance on either foreign-based nationals or local players decreases the odds of finishing in the top four and subsequently winning the tournament. Drawing on social capital, modernisation, dependency, performance and systems theories, the study reveals that there is more to team composition and success at tournaments than the mere inclusion of foreign-based nationals. The study finds a positive relationship between team experience, measured by the number of appearances made in previous tournaments, and team performance. The study provides useful information for coaches, managers, federations and scouts to have a good mix of team composition. Perhaps the playing time or activeness of foreign-based nationals should be considered before their inclusion in the squad. This makes room for future team composition research to consider the skill sets, experience, techniques and knowledge acquired as a recipe for team performance.
keywords: AFCON; foreign-based players; local players; medal; performance; team mix
